modules.summary: Runs on EC2: a head instance and worker instances per run, started and ended by the scheduler (DESIGN.md, phase 5, PR 5).
modules.description:
With `ORCA_RUNNER=ec2` the scheduler starts a run's start `s` as:

- **a head instance** (`--head-type` at registration, else
  `ORCA_EC2_HEAD_TYPE`, on-demand): the dista head, for a pipeline with
  tasks, and the driver, `<binary> resume <run>`, beside it on localhost;
- **`workers` worker instances** (`--worker-type`, else
  `ORCA_EC2_WORKER_TYPE`; Spot with `--spot`), for a pipeline with tasks,
  started straight after with `DISTA_HEAD` at the head's private address.

Each is tagged `orca.run`, `orca.start`, `orca.pipeline` and `orca.role`,
told to terminate when it shuts down, and started from user data that runs
the pipeline's image (`ORCA_EC2_MODE=docker`, the default: `docker run
--network host`, after `ORCA_EC2_PREAMBLE`, such as an ECR login) or the
binary itself (`direct`, for the tests' stand-in EC2), then shuts down
(`ORCA_EC2_SHUTDOWN`). The head keeps the driver's output in the run's
`driver.log` (`<binary> keep-log`) before it does, and if the driver
crashed, fails the attempts it left running with the crash's first frames
(`orca.crash`). Beside its work each
instance runs `<binary> sample` (`orca.sample`; in docker mode as a
container with `--pid host`), whose lines its script uploads to the run's
`metrics/<role>-<instance>.jsonl` with its log (`<binary> put-log`), every
`ORCA_CLUSTER_LOG_SECONDS` and once when it ends, after telling the
sampler to write a last line and stop (`--until`).

With `--worker-procs N` (`auto`: one per vCPU of the worker type) each
worker instance's script starts `N` dista worker processes against the same
head, rather than one, since a process runs one task at a time: each takes
a port of its own, so they share the host. The script notes one that exits,
forwards a SIGTERM to all of them, and shuts the instance down once the last
has gone. Counts and costs stay in instances (`workers`, the budget); a
worker's log is its processes' logs joined.

A pipeline registered with `--workers MIN..MAX` scales: its run starts
`MIN` workers, which may be none, and every tick `scale` reads the head's
demand (`dista status --json`, from port 6390 on the head's private address,
through the pipeline's binary: `<binary> dista-status`, since dista's
sockets can't share orca's binary with flare's) and asks
`dista.scale.decide` what to do. It starts the workers asked for,
up to `MAX`, and drains the ones named with `dista drain`; a drained worker
exits once its work and results have moved, and its instance's script shuts
it down. `ORCA_SCALE_UP_AFTER` (5 s), `ORCA_SCALE_IDLE` (60 s) and
`ORCA_SCALE_STEP` (4) tune the policy. The budget counts `MAX`.

A run is scaled, and its workers are started, as its pipeline was registered
when the run started (`orca.runs.spec`, kept at each start), so registering
the pipeline again meanwhile doesn't strand a live run on settings it never
had; its next start takes the new registration.

A run that needs workers (`MAX` above 0) whose head has tasks waiting and no
worker for `ORCA_NO_WORKERS_SECONDS` (600; 0 turns it off) has the attempt
that waits fail with `no workers joined in 10 min (tasks waiting: N)`, and
its instances terminated. Its driver stops beating with them, so the
scheduler starts it again as it does a run whose process died, until its
retries are spent. Since when it has waited is `orca.runs.waiting_since`,
which the run's page shows. `timeout_seconds` on a step bounds an attempt
whatever it waits for.

A pipeline's secrets (`--secret NAME=ID`) are read by each instance's
script at start, after the preamble, with `aws secretsmanager
get-secret-value` (`ORCA_SECRET_FETCH` replaces the command, which is given
the ID), exported as NAME, given to the containers, and named in
`ORCA_SECRETS` so that every log orca writes masks them.

Every tick, `sweep` terminates the instances of runs that aren't running at
that start, and those older than `ORCA_RUN_DEADLINE` (a day). A head whose
run has just ended is left `ORCA_EC2_HEAD_GRACE` seconds (60) to finish its
script: keep the driver's log, upload its own and its samples, and shut
itself down. Instances get
`ORCA_EC2_DATABASE_URL` as `ORCA_DATABASE_URL` (the control instance's
private address), the warehouse, the logs, the region and the scheduler's
variables named in `ORCA_RUN_ENV`; `ORCA_EC2_AMI`, `ORCA_EC2_SUBNET`,
`ORCA_EC2_SECURITY_GROUP` and `ORCA_EC2_PROFILE` say where and as what they
run. `cpu_millis` is a run's instances' vCPUs, which the scheduler checks
against `ORCA_VCPU_BUDGET` first.

**The warm pool** (`ORCA_EC2_POOL_SECONDS`, 150; 0 turns it off). An
instance's script is then a loop over runs, and the next run of the same
pipeline, started as the same instances, takes its head and workers rather
than launching new ones:

- **The key.** Each instance's row has a digest of what it was started as
  (`pool_key`): role, type, market, AMI, subnet, security group, profile,
  the pipeline's registry hash, and its script but for the first run's
  line, which holds the image, binary, secrets' IDs, the environment it was
  given and its worker processes. A run takes only instances of its own
  keys, so a new registration, image or setting never reuses old ones.
- **Back to the pool.** A head's driver exits; a worker's `<binary>
  pool-wait` (`orca.pool`) sees its run end and the script kills its dista
  processes, which don't end with their head. Each uploads that run's logs
  and samples and runs `<binary> pool-next`, which marks the run's row
  `idle` and beats `polled` every second until it's handed a run. Its run's
  row stays live meanwhile, so idle instances count against the budget (a
  run of the same keys counts them as its own), and `/ops/pools` shows them as
  `idle (pooled)`. A start of a pipeline waits while instances of its keys
  are still on their way there (at most the head's grace).
- **Hand-over** (`_take`). In one transaction, the idle rows of the key
  whose run has ended, that weren't drained and that beat within
  `ORCA_EC2_POOL_LIVE_SECONDS` (5) are locked `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`,
  checked with `DescribeInstances`, ended (`pooled: on to run N`) and
  replaced by rows of the new run (`pooled`); `pool-next` sees its new row,
  records that it `joined`, and the next pass runs it: a new dista head
  process for the head, new worker processes pointed at the run's head,
  secrets read again, and logs and samples under the new run. A run takes
  pooled workers up to what it starts (`MIN`, and what `scale` adds), then
  launches the rest; the others stay pooled.
- **Failure.** One handed a run that hasn't joined within
  `ORCA_EC2_POOL_JOIN_SECONDS` (30) is terminated (`pooled: never took the
  run up`) and replaced: a worker by a new worker, a head by new instances
  for the same start. The sweep ends idle instances after
  `ORCA_EC2_POOL_SECONDS` (`pooled: idle N s, shut down`), those that stop
  beating, and those that don't reach the pool within the head's grace;
  their rows end before they're terminated, so one handed on meanwhile
  isn't. An instance's tags keep its first run; the sweep goes by its live
  row. A run that's restarted, or a worker that was drained, ends as
  before.

modules.summary: Snapshot expiry, the scheduler's half: what orca still needs of a dataset's history, and the binary that does the expiring.
modules.description:
Expiring needs iceberg, which the `orca` binary doesn't link, so it runs in
the project's `orca_maintain` binary (`orca.maintain`). This side decides
what must survive whatever the table's policy says, from Postgres:

- **the snapshots a run that can still go on has read.** A step's reads are
  pinned: a retry or `resume` scans the snapshot the first attempt read,
  so a queued, running, deferred or failed run keeps every snapshot its
  attempts read. (A failed run can be resumed; a succeeded or cancelled one
  can't, and is let go.)
- **the snapshots such a run committed.** A retry finds the commits its
  step made before it was killed by looking through the table's snapshots
  (`orca.tables.find_commit`); one that was expired would be committed a
  second time.
- **every snapshot of the last run that committed to the dataset**, so an
  expiry never leaves fewer than one run's worth of history.

What expiry costs: `orca lineage` and the UI's dataset and snapshot pages
read Postgres only, so they still show an expired snapshot, what made it
and what it was made from; but the snapshot itself is gone from the table,
so it can no longer be read (time travel, `use_snapshot`), and a `rebuild`
reruns the pipelines from the current data, not from it.

overloads.summary: The snapshots of `dataset` orca still needs (see the module doc).
Every dataset orca has committed to, by name.

modules.summary: Fills (#155): a pipeline filling its whole partition range by itself, within limits, set in orca.toml (`orca.config`):
modules.description:
[pipelines.gharchive]
    fills = "all"                # "since_registration", the default
    fill_order = "oldest"        # or "newest"
    fill_max_runs = 2            # fill runs at once, beside its other runs
    fill_budget_per_day = 5.0    # estimated US dollars a UTC day
    fill_window = "22..6"        # UTC hours fill runs may start in
    fill_lag = "2h"              # how long after its end a partition fills

With `fills = "all"` the scheduler queues, on each tick, runs (trigger
`fill`) for the partitions of the pipeline's range that nothing has filled:
from its first partition through the last one that has ended at least
`fill_lag` ago, in `fill_order`, as long as every limit allows
(`fill_status`).

**`fill_lag`** (`0`, the default, for none) is for sources that publish a
partition's data some time after it ends: GH Archive puts each hour's file
up minutes after the hour, so at 00:00 UTC the day that just ended isn't
all there yet. A Daily day D fills from D+1 00:00 plus the lag (on the
schedule's clock), a Monthly month from the 1st of the next plus the lag.
Until then the partition is outside the range, for the fill and for the
coverage alike (`range_keys`), so it isn't counted as missing; the
pipeline page's Fill line says when it fills (`FillStatus.lag_key`). The default,
`since_registration`, is what orca did before: a schedule fills from the
pipeline's registration on, and `orca backfill` the rest by hand.

**What a fill takes.** A partition is left alone when it's done in a run of
any code of the pipeline (every mapped step succeeded for it; with no
mapped step, a run over it succeeded), when a live run has it, or when a
fill run of it was ever queued, so a fill never runs a partition twice:
one whose fill run failed past its retries, or was cancelled, is left to a
person (`orca backfill`, or resume in the UI). Running done partitions
again stays `orca backfill --rerun`. All of that is within the pipeline's
current data version, its steps' `version=` (#297): raising one makes every
partition fillable again, and the fill regenerates them within its limits.

**Limits**, each a reason the pipeline page gives for a fill being idle:
the pipeline paused (by a person or by the watchdog, `orca.watchdog`), the
hour outside `fill_window`, the day's budget, the pipeline's other queued
runs (a scheduled or backfilled run starts first, so fills never starve
them), and `fill_max_runs`. Fill runs don't count against `max_runs`.

**On a worker pool** (`placement = "worker:<pool>"`) the scheduler queues
the fill runs the same way, in the same order and within the same limits,
and leaves them queued, held for a worker of the pool to claim
(`orca.workers`). `fill_max_runs` caps the pipeline's live fill runs
across the whole pool, queued ones included, so the fill never has more
than that many going whatever the number of workers; each worker's
`--max-runs` and its grants cap what one machine takes. A worker pool's
runs cost nothing more than its machines, which run anyway.

**The cost estimate** is conservative, and fails closed. A fill run's
cost is its instances' time (`orca.instances`) at `orca.fleet`'s on-demand
price table, times `COST_MARGIN` for what the table leaves out (EBS,
transfer, requests). The day's spend is that over the fill runs' instances
since 00:00 UTC, up to now. Before starting a run, orca also counts what
the fill runs going and the new one may still cost: the pipeline's
hourly price (head plus its most workers) for the longest fill run of its
last `_HISTORY` (an hour if it has none, at least a minute, plus the warm
pool's idle time on EC2), less what each has run already. A run starts only
if the spend plus that stays within `fill_budget_per_day`. When a price
isn't known (an instance type not in the table, or Kubernetes, whose
cluster orca can't price), no fill run starts on a budget, and the reason
says so. A pipeline whose runs cost money (placed on EC2 or Kubernetes)
starts no fill run without a budget. Runs on the control host or local
processes cost nothing more than the machine already running.

Keyed pipelines and sensors don't fill: `orca register` refuses
`fills = "all"` for them (`fill_refusal`).

modules.summary: The fleet: every machine orca is paying for, as Ops' Pools shows the EC2 ones (`/ops/pools?kind=ec2`, `orca.ui.pools`) and `/api/fleet` has them as JSON.
modules.description:
What the page shows comes from three places, none of which reads the
samplers' files when a page is viewed:

- `orca.instances` says which hosts exist, since when, for which run;
- `orca.fleet_samples` holds each live host's last 30 minutes of samples,
  one row per sample;
- `orca.fleet_hourly` holds, per hour and role, what the 7-day charts add up
  (CPU seconds used and available, bytes in and out), kept 8 days.

The scheduler fills both tables (`ingest`, every `ORCA_FLEET_SECONDS`, 30; 0
turns it off). Run instances upload their samples to the run's `metrics/`
folder (`orca.sample`) every `ORCA_CLUSTER_LOG_SECONDS`, so `ingest` reads
the last lines of each live instance's file from there, a few hundred bytes
of it per instance per pass in effect, and keeps those it hasn't got. The
control instance's sampler (`orca sample --out <file> --keep N`, started by
the stack's user data) writes a file `ORCA_CONTROL_SAMPLES` names, and
`ORCA_CONTROL_TYPE` says what the instance is. Without them the control
instance has no row, unless runs placed on it (`orca register --placement
control`, orca.control) are running, which its row lists; without
`ORCA_LOGS` no instance has one.

Prices are a small table of us-east-2 on-demand rates for the types orca
runs on: an estimate (Spot hosts cost less, and a stopped-and-started clock
isn't modelled). With `ORCA_RUNNER=local` no instance is launched, so the
cost tile says "fixed price" instead and shows `ORCA_FIXED_COST` (free text,
such as `€8.49/month`; "Fixed" when unset), with no region.

modules.summary: How far a dated sensor pipeline is behind the datasets it follows.
modules.description:
A sensor (`orca.sensors`) runs when a dataset it reads, and doesn't write,
gets a snapshot, over the snapshot's partitions. What it follows has, then,
is every partition of those datasets that orca knows of:

- each snapshot a succeeded attempt of another pipeline committed
  (`orca.commits`), holding its step's partition, or the run's partitions
  for a gather step, as the sensor reads them;
- each snapshot the sensor saw otherwise (`orca.sensed`, from `<binary>
  sense`), holding the partitions of the run it started.

Those keys, in the sensor's kind and range (from its start to today), are
what it could have done; `follow` gives each its state as the calendar
does (`orca.calendar`), so what's behind splits into running or queued,
failed, and not queued yet. A single query reads the keys (through the
`commits_snapshot` index), then the calendar's three.

modules.summary: A directed graph drawn as SVG, on the server: the pipelines and datasets that feed each other, and a snapshot's lineage.
modules.description:
Nodes are laid out top to bottom, a row of boxes per level: a node's level
is its longest path from a node with no edge in (such a node itself just
above the first node it points to), and arrows point down. A level holds at
most `PER_ROW` boxes side by side and wraps onto more rows, so the drawing
is about as wide as a phone and grows downward with the graph's depth. In a
level, nodes are ordered by where the nodes pointing to them are, then as
given, which keeps most arrows short and uncrossed. Each node is a box with a
label, a second line, a kind (`dataset`, `pipeline` or `snapshot`, which
the stylesheet shapes) and optionally a link and a class, such as `start`
for the snapshot a lineage page is about. Edges that close a cycle
(a pipeline that reads the dataset it writes, `back_edges`) are drawn round
the right-hand side, back up, and don't move a node down.

modules.summary: Hetzner Cloud's API, as the pool autoscaler needs it (#267, `orca.pool_scale`): make a server, list a pool's, delete one, and the architecture of a server type.
modules.description:
var h = HCloud.from_env()        # raises without a token
    var got = h.create(spec)         # Created: ok, or no stock, or why not
    for s in h.servers("orca-pool=lab"): ...
    _ = h.delete(s.id)               # True if it's gone, already or now
    h.arch("cax31")                  # "arm"

The token is `ORCA_HCLOUD_TOKEN`, or the secret `ORCA_HCLOUD_TOKEN_SECRET`
names (`orca.control.fetch_secret`: `ORCA_SECRET_FETCH` on a Hetzner
stack); it's sent as a bearer token and never put in an error. A call
isn't retried and times out after 10 s: the scheduler calls these from its
tick and tries again on the next.
`ORCA_HCLOUD_ENDPOINT` (`https://api.hetzner.cloud/v1`) is for tests'
fake. Hetzner says a type can't be had in a location now with
`resource_unavailable` or `placement_error`, or `server_type_unavailable`
for one it doesn't offer there: `Created.no_stock`, which the autoscaler
waits on, apart from any other refusal, which it reports.

modules.summary: A run's heartbeat, kept fresh from a thread while the run's steps work.
modules.description:
Steps run on the main thread and can take minutes, so the heartbeat can't
wait for the next attempt to be recorded. A `RunStore` keeps one as a
`Heartbeat[B]`: one thread calls `B.beat` every `interval` seconds, on a
connection of its own, until the heartbeat is stopped or dropped, which
joins it. A failed beat is retried on the next one, after `B.reset`: a run
whose heartbeat goes stale can be resumed elsewhere, and this process then
finds out at its next attempt (see `orca.state`).

**Stopping a step.** A step runs on the main thread and can't be
interrupted there, so the heartbeat thread is also the run's watchdog: on
each beat the store's `Beater` (`orca.state.PgBeat`) also looks for an
attempt of a step declared `timeout_seconds=N` that started more than N
seconds ago, and for a cancel (`runs.cancel_requested`) whose `cancel_at`
has passed, set to `ORCA_CANCEL_KILL_SECONDS` after the cancel by whoever
asked. For the first, the attempt and its step are `failed` ("timed out
after N s") and the run `failed`, with that as its error, so the scheduler
retries it as it retries any failed run; for the second, the running
attempt is `failed` ("cancelled") and the run `cancelled`. Each is one
transaction, with an `orca.audit` row (user `orca`, action `stop`) saying
why, and then the process exits at once, with code 1, taking a local run's
dista head and workers with it. On Kubernetes the Job's pod ends, and on
EC2 the head's script shuts its instance down; either way the scheduler's
sweep removes the rest of the run's cluster, as for any run that isn't
running. A commit the step made before it was stopped is recognised by the
attempt that runs it again (DESIGN.md, "Snapshots"). `SqliteStore`'s beater
stops a step past its timeout the same way, against its file.

modules.summary: `HttpStore`: a run's state over `orca ui`'s API, for a run on a remote worker (`orca worker`, `orca.worker`), which holds no database credentials.
modules.description:
A pipeline binary given `ORCA_STATE_URL` (the UI, `https://...`, or `http`
to this machine only) and `ORCA_STATE_TOKEN` (a worker token,
`orca.workers`) in place of `ORCA_DATABASE_URL` records its run through
this store: each `RunStore` call is a `POST` of JSON to
`<ORCA_STATE_URL>/api/worker/store/<call>` with `Authorization: Bearer
<token>`, which the UI answers by making the same call on `orca.state.PgStore`
(`orca.workers.store_call`), so what is recorded, and every check made on
the way (the run still this process's, not cancelled, its heartbeat fresh
enough to commit), is the same code as for a run that writes to Postgres
itself. Encoded inputs and outputs travel as hex.

**Retries.** A call that can't reach the UI, or that it answers with a 5xx,
is retried as `PgStore` retries Postgres (`orca.store.Backoff`, for
`ORCA_DB_RETRY_SECONDS`); one refused (401 or 403: the token was revoked,
or the run is another worker's now; 409: the run was lost or cancelled) is
final, and the run stops. A fence (`Store.fence`) that can't be made within
half the stale limit refuses the commit, as over Postgres.

**The heartbeat** is a `POST .../beat` from a thread every beat, which the UI
answers with why the run must stop now, if the watchdog says so
(`orca.state.beat_run`); the process then exits, as over Postgres. With
`ORCA_WORKER_PID` set, the beat also checks that the worker that started
this process is still its parent: if it isn't (the worker was killed), the
process exits rather than go on beating, so the server sees the run's
heartbeat go stale and requeues it.

Only `resume`, `status <run>` and `keep-log` work over this store: a
worker's run resumes the run it was given, so `run`, which creates one,
and `status` without a run need the database.

modules.summary: Scheduler instances: two `orca scheduler`s of different images overlapping on one Postgres during a deploy (docs/overlap.md).
modules.description:
With `ORCA_OVERLAP=on`, each `orca scheduler` has a row in
`orca.schedulers`, kept fresh on every tick with the runs its processes
are. One instance leads: it holds the session advisory lock `LEAD_LOCK`,
and only it decides (fires, sensors, retries, starts, alerts, sweeps). The
newest live instance takes the lead: an older one that sees a newer one
live, or is asked to (`orca scheduler drain`), gives the lock up and
drains: it starts nothing, keeps supervising the processes it started
until they end, then ends its row and exits. A run an instance started
records it (`runs.instance`), and `orca.live.held_sql` keeps it live while
the instance lists it, so the leader counts it and leaves it alone.

An instance is live while it has been seen within the stale limit and
hasn't ended; "gone" is the opposite, and only then are its runs, once
their heartbeats are stale too, queued again (`Scheduler._requeue_orphans`).

modules.summary: Keyed partitions: keys that are names, read from a column of a dataset.
modules.description:
```mojo
from orca.keyed import Keyed

comptime Labels = Pipeline[
    "labels", Label, Score, partitions=Keyed["av2.logs", "log_id"], keys_per_run=100
]
```

The keys are the distinct values of `column` in the current snapshot of the
warehouse dataset `dataset` (`ORCA_WAREHOUSE`), each a `Name`. They live in
data rather than in the source because there can be thousands and they
grow. A value that isn't a name, or is null, isn't a key: it's left out,
and `keys` says how many there were on stderr. `--partitions` takes a list of names, `@all` for every current key,
or `@file:<path>` for a list one per line; a range is refused, and so is a
name the dataset doesn't have, so a typo doesn't make a run of nothing.
`<binary> keys` prints the snapshot and the keys, for the scheduler, which
links no iceberg.

A keyed pipeline has no calendar, so `schedule=` and `fills=` don't compile
with one (`Pipeline.check`). This module imports iceberg, so only binaries
with a keyed pipeline build it.

modules.summary: Runs on Kubernetes: a dista cluster per run, made and removed by the scheduler (K8S.md).
modules.description:
With `ORCA_RUNNER=kubernetes`, the scheduler starts a run by creating, in
`ORCA_RUNS_NAMESPACE` (default `orca-runs`), from the image the pipeline
was registered with (`orca register --image`):

| Object | |
|---|---|
| A Job, `orca-<run>-<start>` | the driver: `<binary> resume <run>` |
| A Pod and a Service, `orca-<run>-<start>-head` | the dista head, for a pipeline with tasks |
| `workers` Pods, `orca-<run>-<start>-worker-<i>` | dista's workers, for a pipeline with tasks |

All are labelled `orca.run`, `orca.start` (the run's start count),
`orca.pipeline` and `orca.role`, and the head, its Service and the workers
are owned by the Job, so deleting the Job deletes them. The Job has
`activeDeadlineSeconds` (`ORCA_RUN_DEADLINE`, default a day) and
`ttlSecondsAfterFinished` (10 minutes), and `backoffLimit: 0`, as orca
retries runs itself. The driver reaches Postgres through the Secret
`ORCA_RUN_SECRET` (default `orca-db`, key `url`) in that namespace, and the
head through `DISTA_HEAD`; the scheduler's variables named in
`ORCA_RUN_ENV` are copied to every pod.

Every tick, `sweep` deletes the objects of a run that isn't running at that
start any more, and those of a Job that has finished, first appending its
driver pod's log to the run's `driver.log` under `ORCA_LOGS`: what's left after a
run ends, a run restarted on a new cluster, and what a scheduler that was
killed left behind. Each pod's command runs with the sampler beside it
(`orca.sample`, unless `ORCA_SAMPLE_SECONDS=0`), whose lines go to the
pod's log prefixed `orca-sample `; before a finished Job is deleted, each
of its pods' lines are kept in the run's `metrics/<pod>.jsonl` and left out
of `driver.log`. A pod deleted before its Job finishes takes its samples
with it, as it does its log. Pods ask for `ORCA_DRIVER_CPU`, `ORCA_HEAD_CPU` and
`ORCA_WORKER_CPU` (default 500m, 250m and 1) and `ORCA_POD_MEMORY` (512Mi)
each; `cpu_millis` is a run's total, which the scheduler checks against
`ORCA_VCPU_BUDGET` before making a cluster.

modules.summary: Lineage: which snapshots a dataset's snapshot was made from, and what was made from it, from the reads and commits every attempt records.
modules.description:
```
orca lineage lake.report            the latest snapshot's, back and forward
orca lineage lake.report 4417...    one snapshot's
```

A snapshot that an orca attempt committed is **made** by that attempt: its
run, pipeline, step, partition and code, and the snapshots it read, its
**inputs**. The walks go over those edges in SQL (recursive CTEs):

- **`back`** from a snapshot: the attempt that made it, then the attempts
  that made each of its inputs, and so on, to inputs no orca attempt made
  (sources: a table written by something else, or a read of a dataset
  before it had any snapshot, which isn't listed).
- **`forward`** from a snapshot: every snapshot made by an attempt that read
  it, then what was made from those, and so on.

Both stop at `depth` steps (default 20), so a deep graph is cut rather than
slow. A snapshot recorded by two attempts (a retry that recognised its
earlier attempt's commit) is listed once, as the nearer and earlier. Only
datasets take part: a table outside the warehouse has no name to follow.
The same edges are in the snapshots' own summaries, as `orca.reads`.

modules.summary: Which runs are live: queued, deferred, or running with their process alive.
modules.description:
A running run's process is taken to have died when its heartbeat is older
than the stale limit (`ORCA_STALE_SECONDS`), or, before its first beat, when
the scheduler started it longer ago than the start grace
(`ORCA_START_SECONDS`). A live run holds its partition keys: the
scheduler, sensors, rebuilds and the UI's start queue no second run over a
key a live run has.

**Held by its scheduler instance.** A local or control-placed run started
by an `orca scheduler` with ORCA_OVERLAP=on records that instance
(`runs.instance`, a row of `orca.schedulers`: docs/overlap.md). It isn't
dead while that instance has been seen within the stale limit and lists
it among its runs, whatever its heartbeat: the instance kills a
process whose heartbeat went stale, reaps it, and only then is the run
dead. So while two instances overlap in a deploy, the one that leads
counts the draining one's runs and leaves them alone.

overloads.summary: `ORCA_STALE_SECONDS` (default 30): how old a running run's heartbeat is when its process is taken to have died.

`ORCA_START_SECONDS`: how long a run the scheduler started may go without a heartbeat. By default the stale limit for local runs, and 300 s on Kubernetes or EC2, where a pod or an instance can take minutes to start.

overloads.signature: def held_sql(stale: String, t: String = "orca.runs") -> String
overloads.summary: SQL true for a run of table reference `t` (`orca.runs`, or its alias in the query) that a live scheduler instance holds: a local or control-placed run whose `instance` has been seen within `stale` seconds, hasn't ended, and lists the run among its running.

overloads.signature: def stale_sql(stale: String, grace: Float64, t: String = "orca.runs") -> String
overloads.summary: SQL true for a running run whose process looks stopped: its heartbeat is older than `stale` (seconds, or a parameter such as `$2`), or it has none and was started longer ago than `grace` seconds. `t` is how the query names `orca.runs`: the table itself, or its alias.

overloads.signature: def dead_sql(stale: String, grace: Float64, t: String = "orca.runs") -> String
overloads.summary: SQL true for a running run whose process died: it looks stopped (`stale_sql`) and no live scheduler instance holds it (`held_sql`).

SQL for the keys of pipeline `$1` in a live run, each with the first such run (`key`, `id`): one that's queued, deferred (a step said "not yet", and the scheduler starts it again at its `retry_at`), or running with its process alive. A run whose process died doesn't hold its keys, whatever its trigger, so a backfill or a sensor may queue them again.

modules.summary: Where a pipeline's step functions and dista tasks are defined in its source, so `orca ui` can link each one to its line at the commit a run ran.
modules.description:
orca locate ./build/taxi --root .     # writes ./build/taxi.source.json

`describe` names each function by its module path, `taxi::trips(...)` or
`lake::steps::parse(...)`; the module is a file, `taxi.mojo` or
`lake/steps.mojo`, under one of the source tree's directories. `locate`
finds the file whose path ends with it and the line of its top-level `def`
(or `fn`), and the line declaring the pipeline itself (`Pipeline[` with its
name first), kept as `"pipeline"`. The map, `{"pipeline":
"examples/taxi/taxi.mojo#L243", "taxi::trips": "examples/taxi/taxi.mojo#L42",
...}`, is written beside the binary, and `orca register` records it with the
pipeline's version. Paths are relative to `--root`, which is the
repository's root for the links to work.

The `.mojo` files under `root`, as paths relative to it, skipping hidden directories and `build`.

modules.summary: Where attempts' logs, drivers' logs and runs' timelines go.
modules.description:
With `ORCA_LOGS` set, each attempt logs to
`<ORCA_LOGS>/<pipeline>/<run>/<step>/<partition>/<attempt>.log` (the
partition is `_run` for a gather step, and a keyed one's `/` is written
`%2F`, `orca.name.path_segment`), a run of a pipeline with dista
tasks leaves its timeline at `<ORCA_LOGS>/<pipeline>/<run>/timeline.json`,
and the scheduler keeps a run's output at `.../<run>/driver.log`. Without
it, logs go to stdout only.

`ORCA_LOGS` is a directory, or a location in object storage such as
`s3://bucket/orca/logs` (objectstore's `FileIOResolver`, configured from the
`AWS_*` environment). An object can't be appended to, so for a remote root
a log is written to a staging file under `ORCA_LOG_STAGE` (default
`$TMPDIR/orca-logs`) and `publish`ed when it's complete: an attempt's when
the attempt ends, a timeline when the run does. `attempts.log` records
where the log ends up, which `read_location` reads either way.

Secrets are masked in every log written here: `ORCA_SECRETS` names the
environment variables that hold a run's secrets (`orca register --secret`),
and `mask` replaces their values with `***`.

overloads.summary: `text` with every secret's value replaced by `***`.
`mask`, on bytes that may not be UTF-8.
Whether `location` is in object storage, not on this machine.

overloads.summary: The run's directory under `ORCA_LOGS`, or "" without it.
Where a log bound for `location` is written first: `location` itself on this machine, else its path under `ORCA_LOG_STAGE`.

overloads.summary: Where the attempt's log ends up, `stage_of` it ready to be written; "" without `ORCA_LOGS`.
Copies a remote `location`'s staging file to it; nothing for a local one, which was written in place.

Writes `data` to `location`, local or remote, replacing it, with secrets masked. A local file is replaced whole: written beside it and renamed over it, so a reader (or a `put-log` killed with its instance) never leaves or sees it truncated, as an object's PUT doesn't.
What's at `location`, local or remote; raises if there's nothing.
The time now, to the second, as `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ`.

modules.summary: Machines for a worker pool, from whichever provider the pool names (#267): what the autoscaler (`orca.pool_scale`) calls, so it never knows which.
modules.description:
var p = Provider.of("hetzner", owner)   # raises without its settings
    p.arch("cax31")                  # "arm64": Docker's name, for the image
    var got = p.create(MachineSpec("orca-lab-7", "cax31", "hel1", data, "lab"))
    for m in p.machines("lab"): ...
    _ = p.delete(m.id)

**Hetzner** (`orca.hcloud`): the token as there; a machine is a server of
`ORCA_HCLOUD_IMAGE` (`ubuntu-24.04`), with the project's SSH keys
`ORCA_HCLOUD_SSH_KEYS` (comma-separated names, none by default) and the
firewall `ORCA_HCLOUD_FIREWALL` (none by default), labelled `orca=pool`,
`orca-pool=<pool>` and `orca-owner=<owner>` (the stack's id, so stacks
sharing a project keep their machines apart), which is how `machines`
finds a pool's.

**EC2** (`orca.machines_ec2`): subnets for locations, the security group
and instance profile from the scheduler's settings, Ubuntu for the type's
architecture, the same labels as tags.

Architectures are Docker's (`arm64`, `amd64`), the names an image's
manifest uses, so the autoscaler can tell whether the worker image runs on
a type before it makes one.

modules.summary: A worker pool's machines on EC2 (#267): `orca.machines.Provider` for a pool with `provider = "ec2"`.
modules.description:
- **Where:** a pool's `locations` are subnet IDs, tried in order (each is
  in one availability zone); with none, EC2's default (or
  `ORCA_EC2_SUBNET`).
- **What each instance gets:** the security group
  `ORCA_POOL_EC2_SECURITY_GROUP` (else `ORCA_EC2_SECURITY_GROUP`), and the
  instance profile `ORCA_POOL_EC2_PROFILE` (else `ORCA_EC2_PROFILE`), whose
  role is what its worker reaches the bucket with. IMDSv2 only;
  `InstanceInitiatedShutdownBehavior=terminate`.
- **Its OS image:** Ubuntu 24.04 for the instance type's architecture,
  from the public SSM parameter Canonical keeps
  (`/aws/service/canonical/ubuntu/server/24.04/stable/current/<arch>/hvm/ebs-gp3/ami-id`),
  or `ORCA_POOL_EC2_AMI_ARM64` / `ORCA_POOL_EC2_AMI_AMD64` to pin one.
  `ORCA_SSM_ENDPOINT` points the lookup elsewhere (tests).
- **Tags:** `orca=pool`, `orca-pool=<pool>`, `orca-owner=<stack>` and
  `Name`, which is how a pool's are listed.
- **No capacity:** `InsufficientInstanceCapacity`, `Unsupported` (the type
  isn't offered in that zone) and `InsufficientCapacity` are no stock;
  `VcpuLimitExceeded` and any other refusal are reported.

modules.summary: Table maintenance for a project's datasets: snapshot expiry.
modules.description:
The `orca` binary doesn't link iceberg, so expiry runs in a binary of the
project's own that does: `bin/orca_maintain.mojo`,

```mojo
from orca.maintain import maintain_main

def main() raises:
    maintain_main()
```

which `orca expire` and the scheduler's periodic expiry run (it is found as
`$ORCA_MAINTAIN`, beside the `orca` binary, or on `PATH`). Run by hand it
takes the snapshots to keep besides the policy's with `--retain`; `orca
expire` works those out from Postgres (`orca.expiry.retained`) and passes
them, which is how a run that can still resume keeps the snapshots it read
and the ones it committed.

    orca_maintain expire <dataset> [--older-than 30d|12h|90m|<ms>]
        [--keep N] [--retain ID,...] [--if-policy] [--dry-run] [--report]

Without `--older-than` and `--keep` the table's own
`history.expire.max-snapshot-age-ms` and `history.expire.min-snapshots-to-keep`
decide (iceberg's defaults where unset: five days, one snapshot);
`--if-policy` expires nothing when the table has no
`history.expire.max-snapshot-age-ms`, which is how the scheduler leaves
tables orca didn't create alone. An expiry gives a table orca's metadata
defaults (`write.metadata.delete-after-commit.enabled`,
`write.metadata.previous-versions-max`) when it lacks them, so its own
commit already deletes the old metadata files it drops from the log. `--report` lists `metadata/` before and
after, to count its files.

structs.name: Expiry
structs.summary: What one dataset's expiry did, for the line `orca_maintain` prints.

fields.name: skipped
fields.summary: Why nothing was decided (no policy), or empty.

fields.name: metadata_files_before
fields.summary: -1 when not counted (no `--report`).

overloads.summary: `30d`, `12h`, `90m`, `45s` or plain milliseconds.

overloads.signature: def expire_dataset(dataset: String, older_than_ms: Int64 = Int64(-1), keep: Int = Int(-1), retain: List[Int64] = List(), if_policy: Bool = False, dry_run: Bool = False, report: Bool = False) -> Expiry
overloads.summary: Expires `dataset`'s snapshots: older than `older_than_ms` ago (or by the table's properties when that is -1), keeping at least `keep` (or the table's `history.expire.min-snapshots-to-keep`) and every snapshot in `retain`. The metadata is committed first, then the files nothing retained points at are deleted.
The `orca_maintain` command (see the module doc).

modules.summary: A run's machine metrics on its page: the samplers' files (`orca.sample`) read back, their peaks and warnings, and the charts, drawn as SVG on the server like the DAG.
modules.description:
`read_metrics` reads every `<ORCA_LOGS>/<pipeline>/<run>/metrics/*.jsonl`,
local or in object storage, into one `InstanceMetrics` per file; a line it
can't read is skipped. `metrics_svg` draws them under a lane of the run's
steps, every row on the same time axis (wall-clock time, from the first
attempt or sample to the last), so a step that pegged a CPU or filled a disk
lines up with its bar:

- **cpu**: user and system time as an area, iowait above it, and steal as a
  line, in percent of all cores;
- **mem · disk**: memory used and the fullest disk's used space, in percent
  of the instance's;
- **io · net**: disk reads and writes and network traffic, in bytes per
  second, each scaled to the instance's highest rate, which the label says.

A **warning** is a stretch of samples where memory was over 90% of the
instance's, a disk was over 90% full or CPU steal was over 20%, since those
explain most slow or failed runs. Each is drawn as a band over the steps
lane and the instance's rows, and listed under the peaks.

ends included. A run is over a list of months; a mapped step runs once for
each.

structs.summary: A calendar month, `month` from 1 to 12.

The month after this one.
The month before this one.

modules.summary: `Name`: the partition key of a keyed pipeline (`orca.keyed`).
modules.description:
A name is 1 to 128 bytes of `[A-Za-z0-9._:/-]` without two dots in a row,
such as a log's UUID or a repository's `owner/name`. A `/` separates
segments, so a name doesn't start or end with one or have two in a row.
Neither a comma nor `..` can appear in one, so a list of names on the
command line or in `runs.partitions` reads back unambiguously. Names order
by their bytes. A name has no next or previous name and falls in no date:
it's a `Key` but not a `TimeKey`.

Wherever a name becomes one segment of a path or a URL (an attempt's log,
`/pipelines/<name>/keys/<key>`), it goes through `path_segment`, which
writes `/` as `%2F`; no other byte of a name needs escaping.

overloads.summary: A name already checked; `parse` checks one.
`name` as one segment of a path: each `/` written `%2F`. A name holds no `%`, so this can't collide with another name.
A comma-separated list of names, each once. A range is refused.
Sorts `l` in place, by bytes: a merge sort, as there can be thousands of keys.

modules.summary: Alerts to a person: a push to the owner's phone through ntfy (#184).
modules.description:
A problem is otherwise only visible in the UI. These are raised where
they're decided (the watchdog's trip, a run failing after its last retry, a
fill that stopped moving, the control host's disk, a worker that went quiet,
and `orca notify` from a shell script such as the nightly backup) and sent
as one HTTP POST of plain text to an ntfy topic URL, with the headers ntfy
reads:

    Title, Priority (high | default | low), Tags, Click (the UI's link)

**Settings.** None of these is logged, and none is ever in a message.

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ORCA_NOTIFY_URL` | a topic URL (`https://ntfy.sh/<long-random-topic>`), or just a server (`https://ntfy.example.com`) when the topic comes from the secret. Unset, and no `ORCA_NOTIFY_SECRET`: no alerts. |
| `ORCA_NOTIFY_SECRET` | the id of a secret, read with `ORCA_SECRET_FETCH` (`orca.control.fetch_secret`), holding the topic: a name (appended to `ORCA_NOTIFY_URL`, else `https://ntfy.sh`), or a whole URL. The topic is a secret in practice (anyone who knows it can read it). |
| `ORCA_NOTIFY_TOKEN`, `ORCA_NOTIFY_TOKEN_SECRET` | an ntfy access token for a protected topic, plain or as a secret's id. |
| `ORCA_NOTIFY_MIN_SECONDS` | 1800: the same alert (kind and subject) is sent at most once per period. |
| `ORCA_NOTIFY_TIMEOUT_MS` | 5000: how long a send may take. |
| `ORCA_NOTIFY_FILL_STALL_HOURS` | 2: see `orca.scheduler`. |
| `ORCA_NOTIFY_DISK_PERCENT` | 85: the control host's fullest disk. |
| `ORCA_NOTIFY_WORKER_SECONDS` | 300: a worker holding runs, quiet for this long. |
| `ORCA_UI_URL` | where `Click` goes (`<ORCA_UI_URL>/runs/<id>`, `/ops/control`). |

**Dedup and retries are in Postgres** (`orca.notifications`, a row per kind
and subject), so a restart doesn't send again. `alert` records the alert as
firing and tries to send it; one that failed stays pending and `flush`, which
the scheduler calls on every tick, tries it again after a wait that doubles
(30 seconds, up to 15 minutes). A send is one POST with a bounded timeout and
no retry of its own, and a failure is logged without the URL, so a down ntfy
costs the scheduler at most one timeout a tick, and never an exception.
`resolve` sends a low-priority 'resolved' once, for an alert that was sent.

**Each one is kept** (`orca.alerts`, Ops › Alerts): a row per alert raised
and per 'resolved', with its words, its link, the pipelines and run it is
about, whether it was delivered (`delivery`: pending, sent, or dropped when
a newer one replaced it before it went, with the last error of a try that
failed) and, on a raised one, when it resolved (`resolved_at`, and the row
that resolved it, or a later raise of the same alert). Held-back alerts
aren't sent, so they have no row. Kept 90 days.

modules.summary: Partition sets: which keys a pipeline is partitioned by, from when.
modules.description:
```mojo
comptime Taxi = Pipeline[
    "taxi", Download, Load, Compact, partitions=Monthly["2011-01"]
]
comptime Weather = Pipeline["weather", Fetch, partitions=Daily["2020-01-01"]]
comptime Poll = Pipeline["poll", Poll, partitions=Hourly["2026-11-11T00"]]
comptime Labels = Pipeline["labels", Label, partitions=Keyed["av2.logs", "log_id"]]
```

A pipeline's first step takes its key (`Month` for `Monthly`, `Day` for
`Daily`, `Hour` for `Hourly`, `Name` for `orca.keyed.Keyed`), or a `Seq` of them for a first
gather step. `start` is the first partition: keys before it are refused,
and phase 2's scheduler and backfills count from it. A pipeline without
`partitions=` is `Monthly[]`, with no start.

ranges, keyed partitions lists of names. Only time keys have a calendar, so
only they `fill` a schedule's partition, and only keyed partitions have
current `keys`, read from their dataset.

modules.summary: Pipelines: a named list of steps, checked and run in order.
modules.description:
```mojo
comptime Taxi = Pipeline["taxi", Download, Load, Compact]

var result = Taxi.run(parse_months("2024-01..2024-03"))
```

A pipeline is partitioned by month unless it says otherwise with
`partitions=` (`orca.partitions`): its first step takes the partition key,
or a `Seq` of them for a gather step.

Steps are listed after the step they follow, so the declared order is a
valid run order; `check` asserts it at compile time, along with every edge's
types and unique names. Every function that runs a pipeline calls `check`,
so a pipeline that breaks a rule doesn't compile.

`execute` is the executor: it runs the steps that haven't succeeded yet and
reports each attempt to a `Store`, either `MemoryStore` (what `run` uses: a
run lives as long as the process) or `orca.state.PgStore`, which makes a run
resumable by another process. Each step's output is kept encoded by dista's codec, as Postgres
holds it. A step that raises is retried up to its `retries`, then fails its
partition: the steps after it for that partition, and any gather step over
it, are skipped, while other partitions carry on. One that raises
`orca.step.defer` ends `deferred`, with no more retries, and its downstream
steps are skipped likewise; the run is `deferred` if no step failed.

structs.name: Pipeline
structs.signature: struct Pipeline[name: StringSpan[ImmStaticOrigin], *Ts: StepLike, *, tasks: TaskSet = NoTasks, partitions: Partitions = Monthly, schedule: ScheduleLike = NoSchedule, fills: Fill = Previous, catchup: Bool = True, max_runs: Int = Int(1), run_retries: Int = Int(3), retry_seconds: Int = Int(0), max_retry_seconds: Int = Int(0), sensor: Bool = False, keys_per_run: Int = Int(1), workers: Int = Int(2)]
structs.summary: A pipeline named `name` of the steps `Ts`, in run order, whose steps call the dista `tasks`, over the keys of `partitions`; run by `schedule` for the partition its fires `fills` (`orca.schedule`), and, with `sensor`, when a dataset it reads gets a new snapshot (`orca.sensors`). A backfill puts `keys_per_run` keys in each run it queues, and so do a fill and, above 1, a sensor (#240; orca.toml's `keys_per_run` overrides it): one for time keys by default, tens to hundreds for keyed partitions (`orca.keyed`), whose runs then each go through many keys. On Kubernetes, a run of a pipeline with `tasks` gets a cluster of `workers` dista workers (`orca.kube`); locally it forks `ORCA_WORKERS`.
structs.description:
The scheduler runs at most `max_runs` of its runs at once, and starts a
failed scheduled or backfilled run again up to `run_retries` times, with
backoff: `retry_seconds` (0 for the scheduler's `ORCA_RETRY_SECONDS`)
doubling with each start, up to `max_retry_seconds` if it's set
(`orca.scheduler`). `run_retries=72, retry_seconds=3600,
max_retry_seconds=3600` tries hourly for three days.

with their outputs; they aren't run again. A step that raises is
retried up to its `retries`, then fails its partition. An error from
the store itself is raised: the run stops where it is, and can be
resumed from there. `runtime` is the address of the run's

modules.summary: An EC2 instance's side of the warm pool (`orca.ec2`, `ORCA_EC2_POOL_SECONDS`): the two commands its script runs between runs, through the pipeline's binary, over `ORCA_DATABASE_URL`.
modules.description:
```
<binary> pool-wait <instance> <run> <start>             a worker: until its run is over
<binary> pool-next <instance> <run> <start> <seconds>   until it's handed another run
```

The scheduler hands an idle instance to a run by ending its row in
`orca.instances` and inserting one for the new run, `pooled`, in one
transaction. So the instance learns of its next run from its own rows, and
Postgres, which every instance reaches already, is the only channel: no
other service, port or permission. `pool-next` marks the row of the run the
instance served `idle` (its work has stopped: the head's driver and dista
head have exited, a worker's processes are killed), and beats `polled`
every second, which the scheduler checks before it hands the instance out.
When a new row appears, it records that it `joined`, prints `next <run>
<start> <head address> <0|1>` (the last, whether the run may use new code) and
exits 0; when its row ends with no other (the scheduler shut the idle
instance down), or `seconds` and a minute more pass, it exits 1 and the
script shuts the instance down.

`pool-wait`, beside a worker's processes, exits 0 once the run isn't running
at that start any more, or the worker's row has ended: dista workers don't
end with their head, so this is how a worker knows to stop. Both ride out
a database that can't be reached for a while, retrying every second.

overloads.summary: `pool-wait <instance> <run> <start>`: returns once the run is over for the instance.
`pool-next <instance> <run> <start> <seconds>`: waits, idle, for the run the scheduler hands the instance; see the module's doc.

modules.summary: How a machine the pool autoscaler made becomes a worker (#267): its startup script, and the UI's answer to its `/api/worker/boot`.
modules.description:
The script (`boot_script`, the machine's cloud-init user data) holds one
secret, the machine's own worker token, which orca revokes when it removes
the machine. With it the machine asks the UI for the rest, over TLS:
`boot_answer` gives the worker image (`ORCA_WORKER_IMAGE`, the server's
own), the login to pull it (`orca.registry`), and the variables a worker
needs to reach the bucket (`ORCA_WAREHOUSE`, `ORCA_LOGS`, the `AWS_*`
ones), as the UI's own environment has them. It answers only a token the
autoscaler made for a machine that's live, so a token someone made with
`orca worker-token create` gets nothing from it.

The machine then installs Docker if it hasn't it, logs in, and runs the
image as `orca worker --pool <pool> --name <machine>`, with run cgroups
(`docs/hetzner.md`, "A cgroup per run"). With `ORCA_POOL_WORKER_COMMAND`
set on the scheduler, the script runs that command as the worker instead
(tests, without Docker).

modules.description:
[pools.lab]
    provider = "hetzner"
    machines = [
      { type = "cax31", wait = 600 },   # prefer this; keep trying it 10 min
      { type = "cax21", wait = 600 },
      { type = "cpx32" },               # the last: no wait, keep trying it
    ]
    locations = ["hel1", "nbg1", "fsn1"]
    max_machines = 3
    idle_seconds = 900

A pipeline runs on the pool with `placement = "worker:lab"`, as on a pool of
workers started by hand. `machines` is the order of preference: orca tries
the first type in each location in turn, retries it until its `wait`
(seconds) has passed since it started trying, then moves to the next. The
last type has no `wait`: orca keeps trying it. A machine that's running is
never replaced by a type higher in the list.

modules.summary: The scheduler's part in a worker pool (`orca.workers`): due retries and dead runs queued again for a worker, lost workers' runs, orphans of gone instances, and fill runs queued for the pool.
The pool autoscaler (#267): machines for the pools orca.toml declares (`orca.pool_config`), made and removed by the leading scheduler every `ORCA_POOL_SCALE_SECONDS` (15).
modules.description:
**Demand.** A pool needs a machine while runs of its pipelines (placement
`worker:<pool>`, not paused) have been queued `ORCA_POOL_GROW_AFTER`
seconds (20) that a worker could start: no more of a pipeline's than
`max_runs` less its running ones, and its fill runs. Workers already in
the pool take what they have room for first; what's left waiting is the
demand.

**Growing.** While there's demand, no machine of the pool is still booting
(made, its worker not yet seen) and it has fewer than `max_machines`, the
autoscaler makes one, at most once every `ORCA_POOL_TRY_SECONDS` (60):

- it tries the type it's on (the first, to start with) in each location in
  turn; the first that the provider has is made;
- a type the worker image has no variant for (`orca.registry`: the
  machine's architecture, as the provider says it, isn't among the
  image's) is skipped, saying so;
- when no location has the type, it keeps trying it until the type's
  `wait` has passed since it started, then moves to the next; the last has
  no wait and is tried for as long as there's demand;
- once one is made, or the demand goes, it starts again from the first.

The machine is named `orca-<pool>-<n>`, labelled with the pool and this
stack's id (`orca.stack_identity`, so a project several stacks share keeps
them apart), and booted as a worker (`orca.pool_boot`) with a token of its
own. `orca.pools.status` says what the last attempt came to.

**Shrinking.** A machine is removed (its token revoked, then the machine
deleted, then its row ended with why) when:

- it has run nothing for its pool's `idle_seconds` and the pool has no
  demand;
- its pool is no longer in orca.toml, once it's idle;
- its worker never showed up within `ORCA_POOL_BOOT_SECONDS` (900), or went
  silent for `ORCA_POOL_LOST_SECONDS` (300): its runs are queued again as
  any lost worker's are (`orca.pool_runs`).

**Strays.** A machine of the provider's with the pool's and this stack's
labels that `orca.pool_machines` doesn't have live (made, but the row
wasn't written) is deleted.

modules.summary: Memory pressure (#202): Linux's pressure stall information (PSI) for memory, read each tick, and the admission rule built on it.
modules.description:
some avg10=1.53 avg60=0.87 avg300=0.24 total=1234567
    full avg10=0.00 avg60=0.12 avg300=0.03 total=34567

`some` is the share of the last 10, 60 and 300 seconds in which at least
one task was stalled waiting for memory (reclaim, swap-in, refaults);
`full` the share in which every runnable task was. Meta's TMO acts on the
same signal before memory runs out (Weiner et al., ASPLOS 2022).

**Which file** (`find_source`, once per process):

1. `ORCA_MEMORY_PRESSURE_FILE`, if set: that file, whatever it is (tests
   point it at a fixture);
2. on Linux, the cgroup v2 `memory.pressure` of the nearest cgroup, from
   this process's own up, whose `memory.max` is a limit: in a Docker
   container run with `--memory` that's the container's own
   (`/sys/fs/cgroup/memory.pressure`), which stalls when the container
   reaches its limit even with the host at ease;
3. the host's `/proc/pressure/memory`. Inside a container it is the host's
   (PSI isn't namespaced), which is what a container without a limit
   shares;
4. the own cgroup's `memory.pressure` though it has no limit, for a kernel
   with cgroup PSI but no readable `/proc/pressure`;
5. none: macOS, or a kernel built or booted without PSI (`psi=0`). Then
   nothing is held, and the scheduler says so once.

**Admission** (`Admission`): while `some avg10`, less what runs held at
their own memory limits explain (the most of their cgroups' `some avg10`),
is over the limit
(`ORCA_ADMIT_MEMORY_PRESSURE`, percent, default 10; 0 turns it off), no new
run starts on this host; runs already going go on. The hold ends once
`avg10` is under half the limit, or has stayed at most the limit for
`RESUME_SECONDS`, so a reading that hovers at the limit doesn't flap. A
hold that has lasted `ORCA_ADMIT_PRESSURE_GRACE_SECONDS` (600) with none of
orca's runs going on this host lets one run start at a time (`escape`): the
pressure isn't orca's, and orca shouldn't wait for it forever. The caller
logs and alerts once when that happens (`stuck`).

This module reads files and decides; it keeps nothing in a database, so a
step (`memory_pressure`, from `ORCA_MEMORY_PRESSURE_FILE`, which every run
on the local runner, the control host and a worker is given) and the
per-run cgroups of #201 can use it alone.

modules.summary: Starting processes: what the scheduler needs to run pipeline binaries.
modules.description:
`spawn` forks and executes a binary without waiting for it, its output
appended to a log file if one is given; `reap` collects the ones that
ended, with what `wait4` says they used (`orca.usage`).
`capture` runs a command to the end, killing it past a timeout, and returns
what it printed; `Capture` is the same started without waiting, for the
scheduler to check on from tick to tick. Everything a child needs is
prepared before `fork`, so the child calls only `write` (into a run's
cgroup, on a descriptor the parent opened), `setpgid`, `fopen`, `dup2`,
`setenv`, `setpriority`, `fwrite` (Linux), `execv` (or `execvp`) and
`_exit`.

fields.summary: `wait4`'s `ru_maxrss` in bytes: the largest resident set of it or of a descendant it waited for, one process's, not their sum.

fields.name: cpu_seconds

structs.name: Capture
structs.summary: A command started with its standard output going to a file of its own, to be read when it ends (`capture` waits; the scheduler checks on it from tick to tick). It leads a process group of its own, so killing it kills what it started too.

overloads.summary: Starts `argv` (`argv[0]` looked up on `PATH`), its stdout to a new file under `TMPDIR`, its stderr shared with this process.
How long it has been going.
Whether it has ended, waiting for it if it has (not if the scheduler's `reap` got to it first, which sets `code`).
Kills it and what it started, and forgets its output.
What it printed, once it has ended; the file is removed.

overloads.signature: def spawn(argv: List[String], log: String = "", env: List[String] = List(), nice: Int = Int(0), group: Bool = False, first_to_go: Bool = False, cgroup: String = "") -> Int
overloads.summary: Starts `argv[0]` (a path) with arguments `argv`, and returns its pid. Its stdout and stderr are appended to `log`, if given, else shared with this process. `env`'s `NAME=VALUE`s are added to its environment only, so they're on no command line; `nice` lowers its CPU priority; `group` makes it lead a process group of its own, which `kill(-pid)` ends whole; `first_to_go`, on Linux, makes it (and what it forks) the first the kernel kills when memory runs out (`oom_score_adj` 1000). `cgroup`, a cgroup v2 directory (`orca.cgroup`), is where it goes before it execs: the parent opens its `cgroup.procs` (close-on-exec) and the child writes `0` to it, its first act and an async-signal-safe one, so all it runs and starts is in the cgroup.
The children that ended, without waiting, with what `wait4` says they used.

modules.summary: Requests learned from what a pipeline's runs used (#269): shown on its Resources card and in `orca config show`, and applied where its `cpus` or `memory_gb` is `auto` (`resolve_request`).
modules.description:
From the peaks of a pipeline's last `LEARN_RUNS` successful measured runs
(`orca.attempts.peak_rss_bytes` and `peak_cpus`, #200), `recommend` works out
the request they suggest:

- **memory** is the `MEMORY_PERCENTILE` of the runs' peak memory times
  `MEMORY_MARGIN`, rounded up to `MEMORY_STEP_MB`, and never below what an
  out-of-memory kill raised the pipeline to (`orca.pipelines.memory_raised_mb`,
  `orca.cgroup`);
- **CPUs** are the `CPU_PERCENTILE` of the runs' peak cores, rounded up, at
  least 1; none where peak cores aren't measured (macOS);
- each is clamped to the pipeline's declared range (`cpus`, `memory_gb`),
  saying so;
- an out-of-memory raise lasts while the run that caused it is among the
  `LEARN_RUNS` it learns from: once that many of the pipeline's runs after it
  have succeeded, `expire_raised` forgets it, and the peaks alone decide.
  Without that one unusual run would hold every later run at its size;
- with fewer than `MIN_RUNS` runs there's none.

This is the simplest rule that can work: a percentile over a fixed window,
over all of a pipeline's runs alike (fill, manual or scheduled), with no
decay. The Resources card and `orca config show` show it beside the declared
request.

**`auto`.** A pipeline whose `cpus` or `memory_gb` is `auto` (or `auto..MAX`)
asks for what its runs suggest: `resolve_request` makes the request a start is
admitted and granted with, each time the scheduler or a worker starts one of
its runs, from the recommendation the scheduler caches per pipeline
(`orca.pipelines.learned`, `orca.scheduler.run_request`) and works out again
only when its latest successful run, its out-of-memory bump or its declared
request changes. `auto` is the learned value as its minimum and maximum
(`auto..MAX`: up to `MAX`); with none yet (fewer than `MIN_RUNS` runs, or no
peak cores on macOS), or with learning off (`learn = false` in orca.toml),
that resource has no request, as without `cpus` or `memory_gb`. The run
records where its request came from (`orca.runs.request_source`: `declared`,
`learned` or `default`) and, learned, from how many runs (`request_runs`).

modules.summary: The `orca` command against a deployed `orca ui`, over HTTPS, as a user of it: log in once, then act from anywhere the UI can be reached.
modules.description:
```
orca login https://orca.mlake.dev     # asks for a name and a password
orca --remote orca.mlake.dev backfill gharchive 2025-01-02..2025-01-31
orca --remote orca.mlake.dev pause gharchive
orca --remote orca.mlake.dev status gharchive
orca logout https://orca.mlake.dev    # revokes the token
```

`--remote <url>` (or `--url`), else `ORCA_REMOTE` (or `ORCA_URL`), picks
the UI; without one every command goes to `ORCA_DATABASE_URL`, as it always
has. A bare host is `https://<host>`. Plain `http` is refused but to
`127.0.0.1`, `localhost` and `[::1]`, where nothing is on the wire: a token,
like a password, never crosses a network in the clear.

`orca login` posts the name and password to `/api/login`, which checks
them as `/login` does, under the same limit on failures, and answers an API
token (`orca.tokens`). The password is read without echo from the terminal,
or as a line of standard input when that isn't one (`--user` names the
user then). The token is kept in `ORCA_CREDENTIALS`, by default
`~/.config/orca/credentials` (`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/orca` if set), a line per
UI: its URL, the user, when the token expires, and the token. The file is
written with mode 600 in a directory made with mode 700, and one that
others can read is refused, as ssh refuses a key.

The commands that can go to a UI are `backfill` (`--rerun`, and
`--preview`, which queues nothing), `start`, `cancel` (a pipeline's keys,
or one run), `pause` and `unpause`, `resume` and `rerun` of a run,
`rebuild`, and the reads `status`, `lineage`, `watchdog status` and
`alerts`. An action is a `POST` of
JSON to the path the UI's own button posts to, with `Authorization: Bearer
<token>`, so it's the same code, the same checks and the same row of
`orca.audit` as the button's, from `cli`. Reads are the pages' JSON,
which needs no login, and they send no token. Each prints what the command
prints over the database. The token is never in a URL, an argument or a
message.

modules.summary: Resource requests and grants (#171): runs sized to their share of the machine.
modules.description:
[pipelines.gharchive]
    cpus = "1..16"           # or a count, 4: MIN = MAX
    memory_gb = "2..24"      # GB, decimals allowed: "0.5..2"
    # or "auto", "auto..24": learned from its runs (orca.recommend)

**Requests.** A pipeline asks for a range of CPUs and memory in orca.toml
(`[defaults]` or its own table) or with `orca register --cpus` and
`--memory-gb`. Either can be left out. A pipeline with neither is started
as before: no admission check, no grant.

**Admission.** On the local runner and for control-placed runs, the
scheduler starts a run of a pipeline with a request only if its minimum
fits in what this host's running runs haven't been granted: the host's
CPUs and memory (`host_capacity`: cgroup limits if set, else
`/proc/meminfo` and the cores; `sysctl` on macOS; `ORCA_HOST_CPUS` and
`ORCA_HOST_MEMORY_MB` override both), less a reserve for the scheduler,
Postgres and the UI (`ORCA_RESERVE_CPUS`, 1, and `ORCA_RESERVE_MEMORY_MB`,
1536), less the grants of the runs going there. Otherwise the run waits,
queued, `held` with why (`WAITING`...): "waiting: needs 2 GB, 1.3 GB free of
grants". Runs without a request take no part: they're neither checked nor
counted. `max_runs` and `fill_max_runs` stay as caps on top; with
`max_runs = "auto"` (#266) the grants alone decide how many run at once, up
to its ceiling, and a pipeline with no request to weigh starts one at a time.

**Grants.** A run that starts gets up to its maximum from what's left,
fixed for that start's life, in `ORCA_GRANT_CPUS` and
`ORCA_GRANT_MEMORY_MB`, and recorded on the run (`orca.runs.grant_cpus`,
`grant_memory_mb`, with the request it had). A remote worker (`orca
worker`) admits the runs it takes the same way against its own host, with
the same variables (its reserve defaults to 0 CPUs and 512 MB).

**Learned requests.** `cpus` and `memory_gb` may be `auto`, or have `auto`
as a range's lower end (`"auto..24"`): what the pipeline's runs suggest
(`orca.recommend`), at most the range's maximum, resolved each time a run
starts (`resolve_request`); without one, no request of that resource.
`Request.of` reads `auto` as `cpus_auto` or `memory_auto` with a minimum of
0 and the maximum given (0 for none).

**`"auto"` in `env`.** An `env` value `"auto"` is passed to the run as it
is, for the pipeline to size itself from the grant (`auto_count`), except
`DISTA_WORKER_SLOTS`, which dista reads as a number: orca gives it the
grant's CPUs over the run's local dista workers (`ORCA_WORKERS`), at least
1, or 0 (dista's one per core) for a run without a CPU grant.

modules.summary: The sampler: a run's machine metrics, one JSON line every few seconds.
modules.description:
```
orca sample --out <location> [--pid PID] [--until FILE] [--match PATH]
            [--dirs D,...] [--seconds S] [--count N] [--keep N]
            [--cgroup DIR] [--names DIR]
<pipeline> sample ...                       the same, from a pipeline binary
```

It runs beside every process that does a run's work, started by the runner:
on the ec2 runner by each instance's user data, next to dista (`orca.ec2`);
on the local runner beside each run's process (`orca.scheduler`); on the
kube runner in each pod (`orca.kube`). The runners start it as
`<binary> sample`, since the pipeline's binary is what every instance and
image has; `orca sample` is the same command.

Every `--seconds` (`ORCA_SAMPLE_SECONDS`, default 5; the first line a fifth
of a second after it starts, so any instance it ran on leaves one) it reads `/proc` on Linux,
or sysctls and the Mach host calls on macOS, and appends a line:

```
{"v": 1, "t": 1762250000.123, "dt": 5.0, "host": "ip-10-0-1-5", "cores": 4,
 "cpu": {"user": 61.2, "system": 4.1, "iowait": 0.3, "steal": 0.0, "busiest": 99.0},
 "mem": {"total": 8053063680, "used": 3221225472, "available": 4831838208,
         "cache": 2147483648, "swap_total": 0, "swap_used": 0, "rss": 2952790016},
 "disk": [{"path": "/tmp", "total": 53687091200, "used": 9663676416, "free": 44023414784}],
 "io": {"read": 1048576, "write": 52428800}, "net": {"in": 1310720, "out": 655360},
 "containers": [{"name": "postgres", "mem": 412000000}], "self_cpu": 0.42}
```

- `t` is the Unix time, `dt` the seconds since the previous line.
- `cpu`: percentages of all cores' time over `dt`; `busiest` is the busiest
  core's. `iowait` and `steal` are always 0 on macOS.
- `mem`: bytes. `used` is `total - available` on Linux (`MemAvailable`),
  and app, wired and compressed memory on macOS; `cache` is the page cache
  (file-backed pages). `rss` is the resident set of the run's own
  processes: `--pid` and its descendants, and on Linux every process whose
  command is `--match` (on the ec2 runner, the binary in its containers,
  which aren't the script's children).
- `disk`: per directory the run writes to (`--dirs`, default `TMPDIR` or
  `/tmp`, and dista's `DISTA_SPILL_DIR` and `DISTA_STORE_DIR` when set), one
  per file system, in bytes; `free` is what an unprivileged process can use.
- `io` and `net`: bytes per second over `dt`, summed over whole disks and
  over interfaces other than loopback. `io` is `null` on macOS.
- `containers`: only with `--cgroup`; see below.
- `self_cpu`: the sampler's own CPU seconds so far, for its overhead.

Later fields may be added (CPU counters), so readers ignore keys they don't know; `v` changes only if one
that's here changes meaning.

`--out` is where the lines go: a file, a location in object storage (lines
are appended to its `orca.logs.stage_of` staging file and the whole of it
uploaded every `ORCA_SAMPLE_UPLOAD_SECONDS`, 30 by default, and when the
sampler ends), or `-`, standard output with each line prefixed
`orca-sample `, for a pod whose log the scheduler keeps. The runners put it
at `<ORCA_LOGS>/<pipeline>/<run>/metrics/<instance>.jsonl`
(`metrics_location`).

`--keep N` keeps a file `--out` names to about its last N lines, for a
sampler that never ends (the control instance's, which the scheduler reads
back into the fleet page, `orca.fleet`): once the file has 2 N it's
rewritten with its last N, atomically, so a reader sees either.

`--cgroup DIR` (the control instance's sampler) adds `containers`: the
memory of each Docker container, in bytes, as `docker stats` counts it
(`memory.current` less the page cache's inactive files), read from the
cgroup files under `DIR`, the host's `/sys/fs/cgroup` mounted read-only
(`system.slice/docker-<id>.scope` with the systemd driver, `docker/<id>` with
cgroupfs; cgroup v2 only). `--names DIR` is the host's
`/var/lib/docker/containers`, also read-only, whose `<id>/config.v2.json`
gives a container its name; without it a container is its first 12
characters of id. Reading files, not the Docker socket, keeps the sampler
unprivileged: the socket is root on the host, these mounts are not.

It ends after a last line once the `--pid` process has, or once the file
`--until` names exists, or after `--count` lines. SIGTERM ends it at once,
keeping the lines it wrote (Mojo's runtime threads take signals a blocked
main thread wouldn't, so it can't wait for one), which is why the runners
stop it with `--pid` or `--until`. A line it can't write is dropped with
one message, and it carries on: a sampler never fails a run.

modules.summary: Schedules: when a pipeline runs by itself, and which partition it fills.
modules.description:
```mojo
comptime Taxi = Pipeline[
    "taxi", Download, Load, Compact,
    partitions=Monthly["2011-01"],
    schedule=Cron["0 3 2 * *", "America/New_York"],  # 03:00 on the 2nd
    fills=Previous,                                   # last month
]
```

A fire at some time fills the partition the time falls in on the schedule's
wall clock (`Current`), or the one before it (`Previous`, the default): a
monthly load that runs on the 2nd loads the month that just ended.
`catchup=False` tells the scheduler to start only the latest of the fires it
missed while it was down. The scheduler itself is phase 2's next PR; until
then a schedule is declared, checked, and shown by `describe` and `fires`.
