modules.summary: The scheduler: fires schedules, senses datasets, queues backfills and rebuilds, and starts runs.
modules.description:
```
orca register ./build/taxi             runs `taxi describe`, records the binary
orca backfill taxi 2011-01..2024-12    a run per partition that isn't done
orca backfill labels @all              keyed: runs of keys_per_run undone keys
orca rebuild taxi.trips 2024-01        the pipelines downstream, in order
orca tick                              one pass, then exits
orca scheduler                         a pass every second
```

The scheduler links no pipeline. It knows one by the `describe` it printed,
kept in `orca.pipelines` with the binary's path, and reads the schedule,
partitions and limits from that JSON in SQL. Everything it decides is in
Postgres, so it can be stopped and restarted, or run twice, at any time:

- **A fire is a row.** `orca.fires` is keyed by (pipeline, fire time), and a
  fire's row and its `queued` run are inserted in one transaction, so a fire
  is never made twice. Fires are counted from the last one recorded (or from
  when the pipeline was registered), so the fires missed while the scheduler
  was down are made once each, or, with `catchup=False`, only the latest.
  A fire whose partition is before the pipeline's first is recorded without
  a run.
- **One live run per partition.** Every way a run is queued checks, under
  a lock on the pipeline's row, for a live run (`orca.live`) of the same
  keys: a fire whose partition a live run has records that run as its own,
  a sensor leaves such keys to it (the snapshot's run, if it left nothing
  else), a rebuild's level waits for it, the UI refuses to start one, and a
  backfill skips the key. A partition that's done is run again by a fire,
  sensor, rebuild or start, and its steps append again; `orca register`
  warns of a schedule that fires more than once for one partition.
- **Starting a run is `resume`.** A queued run has nothing done, or what a
  resume or rerun from `orca ui` left it, which is what `<binary> resume
  <run>` takes (with `--allow-new-code` when the resume said so). The scheduler marks the run `running`,
  with no heartbeat and itself as owner, and execs the binary, which claims
  it. It doesn't wait: the run records its own progress.
- **`max_runs`.** Under a lock on the pipeline's row, the runs that are live
  (a fresh heartbeat, or started by the scheduler less than the stale limit
  ago) are counted, and only that many fewer than `max_runs` are started.
- **Memory pressure** (`orca.pressure`, `orca.admission`). On the local
  runner and for control-placed runs, none starts while this host's PSI
  `some avg10` is over `ORCA_ADMIT_MEMORY_PRESSURE` (10%), each queued run
  `held` saying so; then the grants of a pipeline with a request
  (`orca.resources`).
- **Backfills queue what isn't done.** A key is done when every mapped
  step has succeeded for it in a run of the pipeline's current code
  (`DONE_SQL`). A backfill drops the keys that are done or in a live run
  (queued, or running with its process alive: `live_sql`), sorts the rest
  and queues a run per `keys_per_run` of them; `orca backfill` says on
  stderr which keys it dropped and why.
- **Where runs run.** `ORCA_RUNNER` is `local` (a process here, the
  default), `kubernetes` (a dista cluster of pods per run, `orca.kube`) or
  `ec2` (a head instance and worker instances per run, `orca.ec2`).
  A pipeline registered with `--placement control` runs here whatever the
  runner, within the control instance's limits (`orca.control`); one with
  `--placement ec2` waits on a scheduler whose runner isn't `ec2`. One with
  `--placement worker:<pool>` is never started here: a remote worker of the
  pool claims its queued runs over the UI's API (`orca.workers`), and the
  scheduler queues its due retries and its dead runs again for one, its
  fill runs too (held for a worker, `fill_max_runs` across the pool), and
  a run whose worker is gone whatever its trigger.
- **Overlapping instances** (`orca.instances`, docs/overlap.md). With
  `ORCA_OVERLAP=on` a deploy starts the new image's scheduler beside the
  old one: the newest live instance leads and alone decides, and an older
  one starts nothing more, supervises its runs until they end (or kills
  them after `ORCA_DRAIN_SECONDS`) and exits. A local or control-placed
  run records the instance that started it; while that instance lists it
  the run is live (`orca.live.held_sql`), counted against `max_runs`, the
  control slots and the grants, and left alone. Once the instance is gone
  and the run's heartbeat stale, it's queued again whatever its trigger,
  audited.
- **Sensors and rebuilds** (`orca.sensors`). A sensor pipeline's pass
  looks for snapshots of the datasets it reads, in `orca.commits` on every
  tick and from `<binary> sense` every `ORCA_SENSE_SECONDS` (asked in a
  child the next ticks check on, killed after `ORCA_BINARY_SECONDS`), and
  queues a
  run, trigger `sensor`, for those it hasn't seen; with `keys_per_run`
  above 1 the keys go first to its queued sensor runs that haven't
  started, up to that, then to new runs of that many (#240). A keyed sensor's keys
  dataset is sensed too: a new snapshot of it queues the keys that aren't
  done, in runs of `keys_per_run`. Each rebuild queues its
  next level once the one before has succeeded.
- **A snapshot it can't run** is seen all the same. One whose keys aren't
  partitions of the sensor's kind (a week in `orca.partitions`, or names
  for a dated sensor) is recorded in `orca.sensed` with no run and why, and
  the others the tick saw are run. A pass that fails, such as a `sense` that
  exits non-zero, is kept as the pipeline's `sense_error`, which `orca ui`
  shows, and printed once rather than on every tick.
- **Fills** (`orca.fill`). A pipeline registered with `fills = "all"` in
  orca.toml has a second pass after its other runs': runs with trigger
  `fill`, `keys_per_run` partitions each, over the partitions of its range no run has
  taken (`fill_status`), up to `fill_max_runs` beside `max_runs`, none
  while its other runs are queued, it's paused, outside `fill_window` or
  over `fill_budget_per_day`.
- **Retries.** A scheduled, backfilled, sensed or fill run that failed is started again
  after the pipeline's `retry_seconds` (else `ORCA_RETRY_SECONDS`, default
  60) doubling with each start, at most its `max_retry_seconds` if set,
  plus up to a tenth more as jitter, up to `run_retries` times. One whose process
  died (its heartbeat went stale) is started again at once, within the same
  budget. A manual, UI or rerun run is never retried by the scheduler: one
  whose process died ends `failed`, with the error `interrupted: its
  process stopped`, so it can be resumed and holds its keys no longer. A
  run whose step raised `defer` ends `deferred` with `retry_at` the time it
  asked for, and is started again then, whatever its trigger; those starts
  (`deferrals`) don't count against `run_retries`. A run asked to cancel
  whose process died ends `cancelled`.
- **New code.** `orca register` of a new build moves the queued runs to it,
  and the failed ones waiting for a retry that have no step done. A retry
  of a run with steps done by other code would be refused by the binary's
  `resume`, so the scheduler fails it at once instead of starting it, with
  an error (`runs.error`) saying to resume it with `--allow-new-code`. A
  local run whose process exits before claiming its run fails with the
  exit code and the last line of its driver log as its error; one whose
  process crashes after (a segfault, `abort`) has the attempts it left
  running failed with the crash's first frames (`orca.crash`).

The scheduler's clock is `orca.civil.now`, which `ORCA_NOW` fixes; fire
times and retry times are on it. Heartbeats are on the database's clock.
A run's output goes to `<ORCA_LOGS>/<pipeline>/<run>/driver.log` when
`ORCA_LOGS` is set: written there by a local run, published there when the
process is reaped if `ORCA_LOGS` is in object storage, or kept from the
driver pod's log on Kubernetes (`orca.kube`). Beside a local run's process
the scheduler starts `<binary> sample` (`orca.sample`), which writes the
machine's metrics to `.../<run>/metrics/local.jsonl` until the process ends;
`ORCA_SAMPLE_SECONDS=0` turns it off, on every runner. Apart from that, each
tick reads each local and control-placed run's process tree in /proc, and
once the process is reaped its attempts get their peak memory and CPU
(`orca.usage`). `orca scheduler` gives each local and control-placed run a
cgroup of its own where it can (`orca.cgroup`): a memory limit at its
grant, an out-of-memory kill that fails its attempts saying so, and a retry
that asks for more.

modules.summary: Fires and sensors (`orca.scheduler`): a schedule's fires, and a sensor's snapshots, keyed or by partition.
Runs started by datasets: sensors, and rebuilds downstream of a dataset.
modules.description:
```
orca rebuild raw.events 2024-03           every pipeline downstream, in order
```

**Sensors.** A pipeline declared `sensor=True` runs when a dataset it reads
(and doesn't write itself) gets a snapshot. The scheduler learns of one in
two ways (`orca.scheduler`): from `orca.commits`, for a snapshot a
succeeded run of another pipeline committed, and by polling `<binary>
sense` every `ORCA_SENSE_SECONDS` (default 60), for a snapshot something
other than orca committed. `orca.sensed` holds a row per pipeline and
snapshot seen, with the run it started, inserted in the transaction that
queues the run, so a snapshot starts one run however many ticks (or
schedulers) see it. The snapshots a tick sees for one pipeline start one
run, over all the partitions they hold.

A sensor counts from when it's registered as one: the snapshots its
datasets have then are recorded as seen without a run, and commits from
before then are ignored. A backfill or a rebuild covers what came before.

**Partitions.** A snapshot an orca run committed holds the partition of
the step that committed it, or the run's partitions for a gather step. One
committed by something else holds what its summary's `orca.partitions`
says, and without that the downstream pipeline runs the partition its
schedule's next fire would fill now, or, unscheduled, the one now falls in.
`map_keys` moves keys between kinds by containment: a day is the month it's
in, and a month is each of its days. Keys before a pipeline's first
partition are dropped.

**Rebuilds.** `rebuild` queues runs for every pipeline downstream of a
dataset, whether or not it's a sensor, over the keys given, mapped to each
pipeline's kind. A pipeline runs at its longest distance from the dataset
(level 0 reads it), so one that reads two rebuilt datasets runs after both.
The plan is `orca.rebuild_pipelines`; `advance_rebuilds`, on every tick,
queues a level's runs once every run before it has succeeded, and stops at
one that failed or was cancelled, which resuming the run from the UI
continues. A rebuild's commits don't start sensors in pipelines the rebuild
runs itself.

modules.summary: orca's runs in a SQLite file: `SqliteStore`, for single-node orca.
modules.description:
A pipeline binary takes `ORCA_DATABASE_URL=sqlite:<path>` (or
`sqlite://<path>`, so `sqlite:///var/orca/runs.db` is an absolute path):
`run`, `resume` and `status` then keep pipelines, runs, steps, attempts,
reads and commits in that file, through sqlite-mojo, with nothing to
operate. A run killed anywhere is resumed from the file as from Postgres,
by the same `RunStore` code path. The scheduler, the UI and orca's other
commands stay on Postgres (`orca.state.State` refuses a SQLite URL).

The tables are Postgres's, under the same names without the `orca.` schema,
holding what a pipeline binary writes: steps' inputs and outputs are hex
text, times are Unix seconds (`julianday` based, to the millisecond).

**Concurrency.** The file is in WAL mode, so readers (`status`, `sqlite3`)
don't block the writer and the writer doesn't block them. There is one
writer at a time: each change is one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction, which
takes the file's write lock up front, and a writer that finds it taken
waits up to a second (`busy_timeout`), then fails; the owned run's writes
are retried, reopening the file, for `ORCA_DB_RETRY_SECONDS`, as `PgStore`
reconnects. That serialises several runs' processes on one machine, which
is fine for steps that take seconds and rows that take microseconds; it
isn't meant for hundreds of runs at once. Claims are a single guarded
`UPDATE`, so two resumes racing for a run can't both win, and every attempt
checks ownership in its own transaction, as on Postgres. The file must be
on a local disk: SQLite's locks don't hold over NFS and most network file
systems, so two machines must not share one.

`synchronous = FULL`: a commit is on disk before it returns, so a power
loss, not only a killed process, keeps every recorded attempt.

modules.summary: Starting runs (`orca.scheduler`): due retries, dead runs and queued ones, within `max_runs`, memory pressure, grants and the vCPU budget; and a control-placed run's process.
orca's state in Postgres: pipelines, runs, steps and attempts.
modules.description:
Everything lives in the `orca` schema, which `State.migrate` creates and
brings up to date; migrations are SQL in `_migrations`, applied in order
under a transaction-scoped advisory lock, so two processes starting at once
don't both apply one.

**One writer per run.** The process running a run is its `owner` and keeps
`runs.heartbeat` fresh from a thread (`orca.heartbeat`). `State.claim` takes
a run only if its heartbeat is older than the stale limit, or cleared, which
`finish_run` does when a run ends. Every attempt checks in the same
transaction that this process still owns the run, so a process that lost its
run to a resume stops at its next step instead of racing it. The same check
stops a run that was asked to cancel (`runs.cancel_requested`, which `orca
ui` sets) before its next attempt; an attempt already going finishes and is
recorded.

**Each change is one transaction.** Starting an attempt marks its step
running and inserts the attempt; finishing it records the output or the
error on both. A process killed in between leaves an attempt `running`,
which `interrupt` marks failed when the run is resumed.

modules.summary: Steps: the functions a pipeline runs, and the edges between them.
modules.description:
A step wraps a top-level `def` with a name, its input and output types, its
kind, and the step it follows:

```mojo
def download(mut ctx: Ctx, month: Month) raises -> RawFile: ...
def load(mut ctx: Ctx, raw: RawFile) raises -> Loaded: ...
def compact(mut ctx: Ctx, loaded: Seq[Loaded]) raises -> Int64: ...

comptime Download = Step["download", Month, RawFile, download, Mapped]
comptime Load = Step["load", RawFile, Loaded, load, Mapped, after=Download]
comptime Compact = Step["compact", Seq[Loaded], Int64, compact, Gather, after=Load]
```

A mapped step runs once per partition of a run, a gather step once per run.
The edge is checked when the pipeline is compiled:

| Step | Its input must be |
|---|---|
| first, mapped | the pipeline's partition key, such as `Month` |
| first, gather | a `Seq` of the key, every partition of the run |
| mapped, after a mapped step | that step's output |
| gather, after a mapped step | `Seq` of that step's output, one per partition in run order |
| gather, after a gather step | that step's output |

A mapped step can't follow a gather step. Types are compared by their
reflected names, which include their module; the first step's input is
checked by `Pipeline.check`, which knows the key.

A step declares the datasets it reads and writes, as `namespace.table`
names in the warehouse (`orca.tables`):

```mojo
comptime Clean = Step[
    "clean", Month, Int64, clean, Mapped,
    reads=["raw.events"], writes=["lake.events"],
]
```

A dataset in `replaces=` instead is one the step writes whose partitions a
new run *replaces* rather than appends to: `orca.tables.append` and
`append_files` to it make the run's first commit to each partition an
`overwrite` that removes what earlier runs left there, so
`orca backfill --rerun` leaves one copy of a key's rows (`orca.tables`,
"Replacing partitions"). A dataset in `replaces=` counts as written; it
needn't be in `writes=` as well.

```mojo
comptime Load = Step[
    "load", Day, Int64, load, Mapped, replaces=["gharchive.events"],
]
```

A step that fails is tried again up to `retries` times in the same run,
at once, or after `backoff_seconds` doubling with each retry:

```mojo
comptime Fetch = Step[
    "fetch", Month, RawFile, fetch, Mapped, retries=3, backoff_seconds=30,
]
```

A step that can't do its work yet, such as a download that isn't
published or an API that's out of requests, raises `defer(seconds, why)`
instead of failing: the attempt ends `deferred`, spending no retry, and its
run ends `deferred` and is started again by the scheduler that many seconds
later, without counting against `run_retries` (`orca.scheduler`).

`timeout_seconds=N` bounds an attempt: one still going N seconds after it
started is stopped (`orca.heartbeat`), as a failed attempt, and its run
fails, to be retried by the scheduler as any failed run is. A step can't be
interrupted where it is, so the run's process exits: its other partitions
and the step's own retries wait for the run's retry.

`orca.tables` refuses a scan of a dataset the step didn't declare in
`reads`, and a commit to one it didn't declare in `writes`, so the graph of
pipelines and datasets that `describe` gives is what the steps do.

`Pipeline.execute` reports every attempt it starts and finishes, and every
step it skips, to a `Store`; a step's reads and commits reach the same store
through the `Recorder` its `Ctx` holds. `MemoryStore` keeps them in the
process, for a run that lives as long as it does; `orca.state.PgStore`
writes them to Postgres, so a run can be resumed by another process.

binary (`orca.cli`) asks of persistence, from registering the pipeline to
ending its run, so the binary depends on this trait and nothing else.

modules.summary: The control instance's own health: `/ops/control`, the gauges on `/metrics`, and the warning on the home page.
modules.description:
The control instance (Postgres, the scheduler, the UI, Caddy, the apps) runs
a sampler of its own: a container the stack's user data starts beside the
scheduler, with the host's process and network namespaces and the host's
cgroup files and Docker's config files mounted read-only (`orca.sample`
`--cgroup` and `--names`). It keeps its last hour of lines in the file
`ORCA_CONTROL_SAMPLES` names. Every `ORCA_FLEET_SECONDS` the scheduler reads
the file (`orca.fleet.ingest`) and, here:

- rolls the lines it hasn't seen into one row a minute in
  `orca.system_minutes` (CPU, memory, the fullest disk, network: sums to
  average over, and peaks), and one row per container and minute in
  `orca.system_containers` (its peak memory), kept `KEEP_DAYS` (14) days.
  "Hasn't seen" is the newest sample already in a row (`last_t`), so a pass
  again adds nothing;
- appends those lines, as they are, to a file per UTC day,
  `<ORCA_LOGS>/control/<date>.jsonl`, so the history outlives the database
  and can be read back whole. In object storage a file is uploaded whole,
  every `ORCA_CONTROL_UPLOAD_SECONDS` (300) and once its day is over; the
  stack's bucket expires `logs/control/` after 14 days, and a local
  `ORCA_LOGS` has files older than that removed.

A page view reads only those two tables: no file, no bucket. The gauges on
`/metrics` are the newest minute's, left out once it is older than ten
minutes, since a gauge that stays at its last value is worse than none.

modules.summary: Iceberg tables from steps: pinned reads, and commits a retry recognises.
modules.description:
```mojo
from orca.tables import append, scan

def load(mut ctx: Ctx, raw: RawFile) raises -> Loaded:
    var src = Table.load_local(raw.table)
    var batches = scan(ctx, src).to_batches()
    var dst = Table.load_local(OUT)
    var id = append(ctx, dst, transform(batches))
    return Loaded(raw.month, id)
```

- **`scan`** reads a table at a pinned snapshot: the one this step's first
  attempt read, or its current snapshot if this is the first attempt, which
  is then recorded. A retry or a resume of the step sees the same data,
  whatever was committed in between.
- **`append`** and **`commit`** put `orca.*` properties in the summary of the
  snapshot they commit (`Ctx.summary`): pipeline, run, step, partition,
  attempt, commit number, code, and the snapshots read. Before writing
  anything, they look through the table's snapshots for one this step
  already made in this run (`Ctx.made`). If an attempt committed and was
  killed before Postgres heard of it, the retry finds that snapshot and
  returns it instead of committing the data a second time.

A table is known by its location, `metadata.location`, and, when it's in
the warehouse, by its dataset name. `ORCA_WAREHOUSE` is the root of a
filesystem catalog: dataset `nyc.trips` is the table at
`<warehouse>/nyc/trips`, where the warehouse is a directory or a location
in object storage (`s3://bucket/warehouse`, as iceberg's `FileIO` reads it,
from the `AWS_*` environment). **`table`** loads a dataset the step declared, and
**`ensure_table`** creates one it writes if it's missing, and adds the
columns the step's schema has and the table lacks. `scan` refuses a
dataset the step didn't declare in `reads=`, and `append` and `commit` one it
didn't declare in `writes=`. A table outside the warehouse (or with
`ORCA_WAREHOUSE` unset) is used by location as before, and belongs to no
dataset.

**Files written on a worker.** A dista task can write a table's data
files itself and send back only their entries, so the step commits
metadata rather than receiving the rows:

```mojo
def write_hour(day: String, hour: Int) raises -> DataFiles:
    # On a worker: no Ctx, nothing checked or recorded.
    return write_files(load_dataset(EVENTS), fetch(day, hour))

comptime Hour = Task2[String, Int, DataFiles, write_hour]

def load_day(mut ctx: Ctx, d: Day) raises -> Int64:
    var t = ensure_table(ctx, EVENTS, schema())
    if find_commit(ctx, t) >= 0:  # a retry: don't write the files again
        return append_files(ctx, t, DataFiles())
    ref rt = ctx.runtime[Tasks[Hour]]()
    var got = rt.get(rt.remote[Hour](String(d), 0))
    return append_files(ctx, t, got)
```

- **`write_files`** (or a **`FileWriter`**, a batch at a time) writes
  batches into a table's `data/` without committing them, and returns their
  entries as **`DataFiles`**, a dista `Codec` over iceberg's
  `DataFile.encode`. A struct holding a `DataFiles` and plain fields (row
  counts, timings) crosses processes by dista's reflection, with no codec
  of its own.
- **`append_files`** commits entries written elsewhere as one `append`
  snapshot, as `append` commits the files it writes: the same `writes=`
  check, summary and recognition. A retry that finds its commit returns it
  and commits nothing; a step checks `find_commit` first, as above, so a
  retry doesn't have the workers write the files again. Files written by an
  attempt that died before committing them are left unreferenced in
  `data/`, as with an interrupted `append`.

**Replacing partitions.** A new run of a key (`orca backfill --rerun`)
isn't a retry: `find_commit` doesn't recognise an earlier run's commits, so
`append` adds the key's rows a second time. A step that recomputes a key's
rows declares the dataset in `replaces=` rather than `writes=`, and its
`append` and `append_files` to it then replace:

```mojo
comptime LoadDay = Step[
    "load_day", Day, Int64, load_day, Mapped, replaces=[EVENTS],
]
```

- The run's first commit to a partition is an `overwrite` that removes the
  files this run didn't commit from the partitions its new files land in,
  and adds them; its later commits find only the run's files there and
  append. A retry recognises its commits as before, so nothing is
  overwritten twice or lost.
- Another writer's file in such a partition, added after the run's first
  commit to the table, means two runs are replacing it at once: the commit
  raises, committing nothing, and only one run keeps its rows.
- `replace_partitions` and `replace_partition_files` do the same for one
  call, to any table. The summary has `orca.replaced-files` and
  `orca.replaced-records`.

`commit` refuses to remove files that aren't all in the current snapshot,
on every try: a removal planned before another writer replaced them
would otherwise keep both writers' rows.

This module imports iceberg, so only pipelines that use tables build it;
`orca` itself doesn't.

The properties `ensure_table` gives every table it creates, and adds to one that lacks them.
overloads.description:
- `write.metadata.delete-after-commit.enabled=true` and
  `write.metadata.previous-versions-max=100`: each commit deletes the
  metadata files older than the last hundred, so `metadata/` stops
  growing by one file per commit.
- `history.expire.max-snapshot-age-ms` (30 days): the history the
  scheduler's expiry keeps (`orca expire`, `ORCA_EXPIRE_HOURS`). Its
  presence is also what makes the scheduler expire the table at all;
  a table orca didn't create keeps all its snapshots.

overloads.signature: def ensure_table(mut ctx: Ctx, dataset: String, schema: Schema, spec: PartitionSpec = PartitionSpec.unpartitioned(Int(0)), properties: Dict[String, String] = Dict()) -> Table
overloads.summary: The table of a dataset the step writes, created empty with `schema` and `spec` if the warehouse doesn't have it yet.
overloads.description:
A table that exists is brought up to `schema`: the columns `schema` has
and the table lacks, matched by name at any depth, are added in one
schema commit, and a column `schema` makes optional becomes optional.
Rows already in the table read the new columns as null. Columns the
table has and `schema` doesn't are kept, and written as null.

It refuses, with the dataset in the message, what that can't do: a
column whose type differs, a new column marked required, a required
column `schema` leaves out, and a field id in `schema` that isn't the
id the table gave that column, since batches built from `schema` carry
its ids and a column is matched by id first. A new column's id should be
the next one up: the table numbers new fields from its highest id, in
the order `schema` lists them, a struct's fields after the struct.
`spec` is only used to create the table.

`properties` are Iceberg table properties: a table is created with
them on top of `table_defaults()`, and an existing one gets those it
lacks or has with another value (one metadata commit; none when all
are as given). `history.expire.max-snapshot-age-ms` sets how much
history the scheduler's expiry keeps.

No files commits an empty snapshot, as `append` of no batches does, so a step's commits keep their numbers.
overloads.description:
Refuses a dataset the step didn't declare in `writes=`, and an entry
that isn't a data file (a delete file goes through `commit`).

To a dataset the step declared in `replaces=`, it's
`replace_partition_files`.

overloads.signature: def append_files(mut ctx: Ctx, mut table: Table, files: DataFiles) -> Int64
overloads.summary: `append_files` of the entries a task returned.

overloads.signature: def commit(mut ctx: Ctx, mut table: Table, operation: String, var files: FileChanges) -> Int64
overloads.summary: Commits `files` (data files added and removed, already written) to `table` as one snapshot of `operation`, e.g. `replace` for a compaction, and returns its ID, or returns the snapshot an earlier attempt of this step committed.
overloads.description:
Every file `files` removes must be in the table's current snapshot, on
the first try and on each retry after another writer committed first:
if one isn't, another writer removed or replaced it since the caller
read it, and the commit raises, committing nothing, rather than remove
the rest and keep both writers' rows. The step's retry plans the change
again. (`replace_partitions` plans it again itself on each try.)

overloads.signature: def replace_partitions(mut ctx: Ctx, mut table: Table, batches: List[RecordBatch]) -> Int64
overloads.summary: Writes `batches` to `table` as one snapshot that also removes the files earlier runs left in the partitions the rows land in, and returns its ID, or the snapshot an earlier attempt of this step committed.
overloads.description:
What `append` does to a dataset the step declared in `replaces=`; this
is for a table outside the warehouse, or a step that replaces one table
and appends to another it declares in `writes=`.

- The run's first commit to a partition is an `overwrite` that removes
  every data and delete file in it that this run didn't commit, and
  adds the new files. Later commits of the run to the partition find
  only its own files there and append; files of this run, from any of
  its steps and attempts, are never removed.
- The partitions are those of the new files under the table's current
  spec: no rows replace nothing. Files written under an older spec are
  left alone. An unpartitioned table is one partition: the run replaces
  the whole table.
- What to remove is planned against the snapshot each try commits on
  top of, again on every retry after another writer committed first.
- A file in a partition being replaced that another writer committed
  after this run's first commit to the table means two writers are
  replacing (or writing) the partition at once. The commit raises,
  committing nothing, so only one of them keeps its rows: the other's
  attempt fails, and a rerun of it once the first has finished replaces
  the partition again.

The snapshot's summary has `orca.replaced-files` and
`orca.replaced-records`: the data files and rows it removed.

overloads.signature: def replace_partition_files(mut ctx: Ctx, mut table: Table, files: List[DataFile]) -> Int64
overloads.summary: `replace_partitions` of data files already written, here or on a worker (`write_files`), as `append_files` commits them.

overloads.signature: def replace_partition_files(mut ctx: Ctx, mut table: Table, files: DataFiles) -> Int64
overloads.summary: `replace_partition_files` of the entries a task returned.

modules.summary: The dista tasks a pipeline's steps call, and the runtime a run gets.
modules.description:
```mojo
comptime Square = Task[Int, Int, square]
comptime TaxiTasks = Tasks[Square]
comptime Taxi = Pipeline["taxi", Download, Load, tasks=TaxiTasks]

def load(mut ctx: Ctx, raw: RawFile) raises -> Loaded:
    ref rt = ctx.runtime[TaxiTasks]()
    var r = rt.remote[Square](7)
    ...
```

A run of a pipeline with tasks starts one dista `Runtime` before its first
step and keeps it until the run ends: in local mode it forks a head and
`ORCA_WORKERS` workers (default 4); with `DISTA_HEAD` set it joins that
cluster instead. The same binary is dista's worker: run with `DISTA_ROLE`
set, `orca_main` hands the process to dista before reading its arguments.

The runtime starts before orca opens a database connection or its heartbeat
thread, so the forked head and workers inherit neither.

A driver or worker given `DISTA_HEAD` first waits until the head accepts a
connection (`wait_for_head`), trying for a second at a time. On Kubernetes
the head's Service can be a moment old: a connection sent before the node
routes its address waits on a connection-tracking entry that never routes,
for minutes, and dista connects without a timeout. A fresh try each second
gets a fresh entry.

modules.summary: A run's Dista timeline and its workers over time, drawn as SVG on the server for the run's page.
modules.description:
The timeline is dista's, in Chrome's trace format: a `process_name` event
names each worker's lane (`pid`), and each task is an `X` event on thread 1
(running) or 2 (waiting for inputs), with `ts` and `dur` in microseconds.
Each worker is one lane; a task is a bar coloured by its name, and the time
a task waited for its inputs a thin bar under it. Perfetto shows the same
file in full; this is the glance.

The worker count comes from `orca.instances`, which an `ec2` run has: one
step per instance started or ended.

modules.summary: API tokens: what `orca login` gets from `orca ui`, so the `orca` command on another machine can act as a user of it (`orca.remote`).
modules.description:
```
orca user tokens alice          her tokens: label, created, last used, expires
orca user revoke alice 3        or @all
```

A token is `orca_` and 64 hex digits, 32 random bytes from the system's
generator; the prefix lets a secret scanner recognise one that leaked. The
UI gives it out once, to `POST /api/login` with the right password, and
keeps only its SHA-256 digest in `orca.api_tokens`, with its user, a label
(the machine that logged in), when it was made and last used, and when it
expires: `ORCA_API_TOKEN_DAYS` (default 30) days on, or fewer if the login
asked for fewer. A request sends it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`;
one that's unknown, expired or revoked is answered 401. `orca logout`
revokes its own (`POST /api/logout`), `orca user revoke` any of a user's,
and changing a user's password or removing the user revokes all of hers,
as it ends her sessions (`orca.auth`).

fields.summary: Empty if it hasn't been.

How many days a new token lasts: `asked` if it's from 1 to the most allowed, `ORCA_API_TOKEN_DAYS` (default 30, at most 3650), else that most. Raises for a setting that isn't a count of days.
A token's label as it's kept: printable ASCII, at most `MAX_LABEL` bytes, `-` for anything else, and `cli` for none.

modules.summary: The TOML that `orca.toml` is written in (`orca.config`): a parser and a writer for the subset a configuration file needs.
modules.description:
var doc = parse_toml(text)          # raises "<line>: <why>" on bad input
    doc.get(["pipelines", "gharchive", "workers"])   # Optional[TomlValue]
    doc.tables(["pipelines"])           # the tables directly under it

Supported, as TOML 1.0 has them: comments, `[table]` headers with bare,
quoted and dotted keys, `key = value` with dotted keys, basic strings (with
every escape) and literal strings, integers (decimal, with `_` between
digits), floats, booleans, arrays of those (over several lines, with
comments and a trailing comma), inline tables, nested, and arrays of inline
tables, inline (`machines = [{ type = "cax31", wait = 600 }, ...]`) or as
`[[x]]` headers, nested too (`[[version.step]]` adds to the last
`[[version]]`). A key or table
defined twice, a dotted key extending a table a header defined, and a header
reopening an inline table are refused, as TOML refuses them. Not supported,
each refused with a message saying so: multi-line strings, dates and times, hexadecimal, octal and binary integers,
`inf` and `nan`, arrays of arrays, arrays mixing tables with other values,
and keys holding control characters.

The document is flat: an entry per table and per value, in the order the
file has them, each with its whole key path, so a reader looks values up by
path and a new key needs no new type. An array of tables is an `ARRAY`
entry whose items are its elements' indices, of kind `TABLE`, and each
element a table at the array's path and its index: `machines.0.type`. mojoshelf's `mojo-toml` is built for
Mojo before 1.0, which is why orca has its own.

modules.summary: Time zones, from the system's TZif files (RFC 8536).
modules.description:
```mojo
var ny = Zone.load("America/New_York")
var offset = ny.offset_at(utc(2024, 7, 1))   # -14400, EDT
```

A TZif file of version 2 or later lists the zone's transitions as 64-bit
times, each with the UTC offset in force from then on, and ends with a POSIX
`TZ` string (`EST5EDT,M3.2.0,M11.1.0`) that gives the rule after the last
transition. "Slim" files, which some systems install, list transitions only
up to when the current rule began and rely on that string for every year
since; "fat" ones list them to 2037. `Zone` reads both, and a version 1 file,
which has only 32-bit times and no rule. Leap-second records are skipped:
orca's times are POSIX times, as the `right/` zones' aren't.

Files are read from `ORCA_ZONEINFO`, default `/usr/share/zoneinfo`. `UTC`
needs no file.

modules.summary: A release's upgrade steps (#323): what has to be done before or after a deploy, which a project's image ships in `upgrade.toml` and the Hetzner deploy shows or runs (`deploy/hetzner/deploy.sh`).
modules.description:
```toml
[[version]]
version = "1.2.0"

[[version.step]]
id = "1.2.0-retool"      # unique and stable
when = "after"           # before | after (the default)
run = "orca backfill --rerun mojo_retool @all"   # an orca command

[[version.step]]
id = "1.1.0-egress-hf"
when = "before"
manual = "The console downloads its model from huggingface.co: allow outbound HTTPS."
```

`orca upgrade --from <deployed> --to <new>` prints the steps of every
version after `--from` up to `--to`, a line each:

    step<TAB><id><TAB><before|after><TAB><run|manual><TAB><command or text>

What makes a step run once is that range: a deploy from 1.1.0 to 1.2.0 takes
1.2.0's steps, and the next deploy, from 1.2.0, doesn't. Nothing is recorded
in the database. A `--from` that isn't a version (a commit, empty) takes
only `--to`'s steps.

`orca upgrade [--file F] [--from V] --to V [--when before|after]`.

modules.summary: What a run's processes use: each attempt's peak memory and CPU.
modules.description:
Whoever starts a run's process measures it: the scheduler for a local or
control-placed run (`orca.scheduler`), `orca worker` for a remote worker's
(`orca.worker`). Each tick, at most every quarter of a second, it reads
the process's tree in /proc (`orca.sample.tree_usage`: the driver and what
it started, dista's local workers among them) and keeps a `Meter` of it:
the resident bytes, the CPU seconds so far (utime + stime, with what the
tree's processes waited for), and the cores that kept busy since the
sample before. When the process is reaped, `wait4` adds its own word:
`ru_maxrss`, the largest single process (a lower bound on the tree's), and
its CPU seconds, which count descendants that ended after the last sample.

A process runs every attempt of a run's start, so its samples are shared
out among those attempts by time (`attribute`): an attempt's peak is the
largest sample taken while it ran (or, for one shorter than a tick, the
sample just after it), its CPU the meter's CPU at its end less at its
start, its peak cores the busiest interval it overlapped. `ru_maxrss`
raises the peak of a process's only attempt. A meter keeps at most
`MAX_MARKS` samples, merging neighbours as it fills (keeping their maximum
and the later total), so a long run's samples are coarser, not dropped.

On macOS, which has no /proc, there are no samples: a process's only
attempt gets `wait4`'s numbers, and none gets its peak cores; a process
of several attempts records none. Runs on EC2 or Kubernetes, and runs no
scheduler or worker started (`<binary> run` by hand), record nothing:
their columns stay NULL.

The numbers are `orca.attempts`' `peak_rss_bytes`, `cpu_seconds` and
`peak_cpus` (migration 35), written once, when the process ends: by the
scheduler over Postgres, and for a worker's run by `orca ui`, which the
worker sends its meter with `/api/worker/exited` (`marks_json`, ages in
seconds before the request, so neither clock needs to agree with the
database's).

aliases.summary: The most samples a meter keeps; past it, neighbours are merged.

aliases.name: MIN_SAMPLE_SECONDS

modules.summary: A dataset's current snapshot, read from its table's metadata file without iceberg, for `<binary> sense`.
modules.description:
A dataset `ns.table` is the filesystem catalog's table at
`<ORCA_WAREHOUSE>/ns/table`, as in `orca.tables`. Its current metadata file
is the one `metadata/version-hint.text` names, or else the highest version
under `metadata/`, ties broken by `last-updated-ms`, as iceberg's catalog
finds it. Of that file, `current_snapshot` reads the current snapshot's ID
and two properties of its summary: whether an orca step made it
(`orca.run`), and the partition keys it holds (`orca.partitions`), which a
writer that isn't orca can set too.

The warehouse is a directory or a location in object storage
(`s3://bucket/warehouse`), listed and read through objectstore's
`FileIOResolver`, from the `AWS_*` environment.

orca's pipelines import iceberg only if they use tables, and every binary
answers `sense`, so this reads the JSON itself: just enough of it to walk
objects and arrays to the fields it needs.

modules.summary: The watchdog: pauses pipelines when something leaves a sane range.
modules.description:
On 2026-11-05 nothing noticed ~360 EC2 launches in 38 minutes, or a run
waiting three hours for workers that never came. The scheduler evaluates
these rules every `ORCA_WATCHDOG_SECONDS` (60; 0 turns the watchdog off),
each from Postgres only (never object storage), with the thresholds below
(each rule's environment variable overrides its default):

| Rule | Trips when | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| `launches` | more than `ORCA_WATCHDOG_LAUNCHES` (200) instances were launched in the last hour (pool handovers aren't launches) | all pipelines |
| `cost` | the estimated cost of the instances up (`orca.fleet`'s price table) stayed over `ORCA_WATCHDOG_COST_HOUR` ($3) an hour for `ORCA_WATCHDOG_COST_MINUTES` (15) minutes, or the last 24 hours cost over `ORCA_WATCHDOG_COST_DAY` ($25) | all pipelines |
| `idle` | at least `ORCA_WATCHDOG_IDLE_WORKERS` (4) workers, up for `ORCA_WATCHDOG_IDLE_MINUTES` (10, at most 30) minutes, averaged under `ORCA_WATCHDOG_IDLE_CPU` (15) percent CPU over them (pooled idle and draining workers aren't counted) | the pipelines owning those workers |
| `failing` | a pipeline had more than `ORCA_WATCHDOG_FAILED` (20) failed attempts in the last hour, or at least `ORCA_WATCHDOG_FAILED_MIN` (10) attempts ended and more than `ORCA_WATCHDOG_FAILED_PERCENT` (50) percent failed | each such pipeline |
| `stuck` | a run with a running attempt, on instances that are sampled, has had no attempt start or end, no instance launched or ended and no sampled host over `ORCA_WATCHDOG_STUCK_CPU` (5) percent CPU for `ORCA_WATCHDOG_STUCK_MINUTES` (30, at most 30, since samples are kept that long) minutes | that run's pipeline |
| `control` | the control instance's newest minute has memory over `ORCA_WATCHDOG_MEMORY` (90) percent or its fullest disk over `ORCA_WATCHDOG_DISK` (85) | all pipelines |

A tripped rule **pauses** its scope through `orca.pause.set_paused`
(what the UI's Pause button does; pipelines already paused are left
alone), writes an `orca.audit` row per pipeline (user `watchdog`, the
rule's numbers), and a row of `orca.watchdog_trips`, which the banner on
`/`, `/ops/pools` and `/ops/control`, `/watchdog` and `/metrics` show for as long as any of its
pipelines is paused. It never resumes anything. A rule that is still over
its limit when a pipeline is unpaused trips again on the next pass, so
snooze it (`orca watchdog snooze <rule> 2h`, or on `/watchdog`) first;
that is stored in `orca.watchdog_rules` and audited.

A rule checks one threshold or more (`limits`: `control` checks memory
and disk, `cost` the sustained rate and the day, `failing` the count and
the share, `idle` the CPU and the number of workers). Each reading keeps
every check's value and limit and whether it is past it, and so does each
trip, so `orca watchdog status`, `/watchdog` and `/api/watchdog` show
every threshold and which one tripped.

Evaluation is pure (`eval_*`, over plain rows) apart from the gathering
(`gather_*`).

modules.summary: `orca worker`: runs a pool's runs on this machine, talking only to `orca ui`'s API.
modules.description:
```
ORCA_WORKER_TOKEN=orca_... orca worker --pool bgent --remote https://orca.mlake.dev
```

Every `--poll-seconds` (2) the worker posts its heartbeat to
`/api/worker/claim` (`orca.workers`), its name, image, CPUs, memory and
the runs it has, and, while it has fewer than `--max-runs` (1), asks for
one. A run it's given starts as the local runner starts one: the
pipeline's binary (the path it was registered with, which the worker's
image has too) with `resume <run>`, in a process group of its own, its
output staged under `--dir` (`$TMPDIR/orca-worker`), with the pipeline's
`env`, its secrets read here with `ORCA_SECRET_FETCH` and named in
`ORCA_SECRETS`, and `ORCA_STATE_URL` and `ORCA_STATE_TOKEN` in place of a
database: the run records itself over the API (`orca.http_store`). Its
data and logs go where the worker's own `ORCA_WAREHOUSE` and `ORCA_LOGS`
say, as any run's do. When the process ends, its output is appended to
the run's `driver.log` by `<binary> keep-log`, which also fails the
attempts a crash left running; a process that ended before claiming its
run has the run failed, saying why (`/api/worker/exited`). Beside each
run's process it starts `<binary> sample` (`orca.sample`, unless
`ORCA_SAMPLE_SECONDS=0`), which writes this machine's metrics to
`<ORCA_LOGS>/<pipeline>/<run>/metrics/worker-<name>.jsonl`, so the run's
page has its Machines card, as a local run's does. Each poll the
worker samples its runs' process trees, as the scheduler samples a local
run's, and sends the samples with `/api/worker/exited`, so their attempts
get their peak memory and CPU (`orca.usage`). Where the worker can make
cgroups (`orca.cgroup`), each run gets one at its grant, and an
out-of-memory kill is reported with `/api/worker/exited`, which fails the
attempts saying so and raises what the pipeline asks for.

**No database.** The worker refuses to start with `ORCA_DATABASE_URL` set:
nothing on a worker holds database credentials. Its token is
`ORCA_WORKER_TOKEN`, or the first line of `--token-file`; one that's
revoked, expired or for another pool than `--pool` is refused, and the
worker exits (code 3).

**Versions.** The worker's image is `--image`, else `ORCA_IMAGE`. A run it's
given whose pipeline's image isn't that is put back (`/api/worker/release`)
rather than started, though the UI shouldn't hand it one
(`orca.workers.version_refusal`).

**Dying.** A worker that's killed takes its runs with it: each run's
heartbeat thread exits its process once its parent isn't the worker
(`ORCA_WORKER_PID`), so the run's heartbeat goes stale and the scheduler
queues it again, for this worker or another, whatever its trigger
(`orca.scheduler`'s `_requeue_lost`); a run this worker claimed and never
started has its start given back.

modules.summary: Remote workers, the server's side: worker tokens, claims, and the store calls a worker's runs make over `orca ui` (`orca.http_store`).
modules.description:
```
orca worker-token create --pool bgent [--days N] [--label L]   prints the token once
orca worker-token list                                          id, pool, label, worker, last seen
orca worker-token revoke <id>
```

A pipeline placed `worker:<pool>` (`placement` in orca.toml, or `orca
register --placement worker:<pool>`) has its runs started by a worker of
that pool (`orca worker`, `orca.worker`), never by the scheduler, which
keeps them queued, `held` "waiting for a worker of pool <pool>", requeues
one whose heartbeat went stale (a worker that died, or a laptop that went
to sleep) as it would start any dead run again, and fails one that has no
retries left. A run whose worker is gone (not seen for half the stale
limit, or seen since without it) is queued again whatever its trigger. A
pipeline with `fills = "all"` has its fill runs queued the same way, held
for a worker, at most `fill_max_runs` of them queued or running across the
pool (`orca.fill`).

**Tokens.** A worker token is an API token (`orca.tokens`: `orca_` and 64
hex digits, kept only as its SHA-256), in `orca.workers` rather than
`orca.api_tokens`, scoped to one pool: it can claim that pool's runs and
make the store calls of the runs it claimed, and nothing else; a user's
token gets nothing here, and a worker token gets nothing elsewhere. It
lasts `--days` (default and at most `ORCA_WORKER_TOKEN_DAYS`, 365). A
revoked token stays listed, as revoked, and is answered 401.

**The API** (`orca.api.worker`): `/api/worker/claim`, the worker's
heartbeat and its claims; `/api/worker/release`, a run it won't start;
`/api/worker/exited`, a run's process ended; `/api/worker/store/<call>`,
`store_call`, a `RunStore` call of a run it claimed.

A claim takes, under its pipeline's lock, a queued run whose pipeline isn't
paused and has fewer than `max_runs` live runs (a fill run: fewer than
`fill_max_runs` running fill runs, inside its `fill_window`, with fills on),
its other runs before its fill runs (the oldest of each pipeline's, so one
pipeline's queue at its cap never holds up another's), and starts it as the
scheduler starts a run: `running`, owner `worker`, no heartbeat yet (the
run's process claims it, within the start grace), one more start. Each
claim is a row of `orca.audit` (user `worker:<label>`, source `worker`).
**Versions.** A run needs its pipeline's image (`--image`, `image` in
orca.toml) to be the worker's (`ORCA_IMAGE`), both empty included: a worker
of another image isn't given it, and it stays queued, held saying why. The
worker checks the spec again before it starts anything (`orca.worker`).

| Module | |
|---|---|
| `orca.api.pipelines` | a pipeline, a keyed one's counts, Start runs' preview |
| `orca.api.runs` | a run, a list's page, a code version, a run's machines |
| `orca.api.datasets` | rebuilds and lineage |
| `orca.api.ops` | `/api/fleet`, `/api/workers`, `/api/system`, `/api/gantt`, `/api/watchdog` |

modules.summary: The actions: each a `POST` of a form (or of JSON, from `orca --remote`) that changes something, through `orca.actions`.
modules.description:
| `POST` | |
|---|---|
| `/pipelines/<name>/runs` | start a run over `partitions` |
| `/pipelines/<name>/backfill` | a run per partition in `partitions` that has none; `rerun=1` for done ones too |
| `/pipelines/<name>/cancel` | cancel its queued, running and retrying runs over `partitions` (`@all` or empty: all) |
| `/pipelines/<name>/pause`, `/unpause` | stop the scheduler starting its runs, or let it again |
| `/watchdog/<rule>/snooze` | silence a watchdog rule for `duration` (`2h`, `30m`, `1d`; `off` ends it) |
| `/watchdog/<trip>/ack`, `/watchdog/all/ack` | acknowledge a watchdog trip, or all of them |
| `/runs/<id>/resume` | queue a failed, cancelled or stalled run again; `allow_new_code=1` confirms new code |
| `/runs/<id>/rerun` | a new run from `step` on, the steps before it copied |
| `/runs/<id>/cancel` | cancel a run, before its next attempt if it's running |
| `/runs/bulk` | `do=cancel`, `retry` or `backfill` the runs picked from a list: each `pick=<id>`, or with `all=1` every run its filters (`view`, `pipeline`, `status`, ...) match, if there are still `expect` of them |
| `/datasets/<name>/rebuild` | rebuild every pipeline downstream over `partitions` |

Each answers `303 See Other` to the page of what it made (a script gets
that page's JSON, with 200), or 409 saying why it wasn't done, with a way
to confirm when it asks for one. `orca.web.server` checks the session and
audits each one done as its user's.

modules.summary: The worker API: what `orca worker` (`orca.worker`) and the runs it starts (`orca.http_store.HttpStore`) call, each a `POST` of JSON with `Authorization: Bearer <worker token>`. What each call does is `orca.workers`; this is how a request reaches it.
modules.description:
| Path | |
|---|---|
| `/api/worker/claim` | the worker's heartbeat, and with `slots` > 0 a queued run of its pool to start: its spec, or `null` |
| `/api/worker/release` | a run it was given and won't start: queued again, held saying why |
| `/api/worker/exited` | a run's process ended, with its samples |
| `/api/worker/boot` | a machine the pool autoscaler made, booting: the image, its login and the bucket's variables (`orca.pool_boot`) |
| `/api/worker/store/<call>` | a `RunStore` call of a run this worker claimed (`orca.state.PgStore`) |

Every call is checked the same way first: the token is a live worker
token (401), the body a JSON object (400), and a `pool` it names the
token's (403). A user's API token gets nothing here, and a worker token
nothing elsewhere.

**Its own listener.** By default `orca ui` answers these with its pages.
With `ORCA_WORKER_ADDR` (`host:port`) it also serves them on that address,
from a thread of their own, so a slow page can't hold up a worker's claims
and heartbeats or its runs' store calls: point `orca worker --remote` at
it. Everything else there is 404.

modules.summary: orca's pages: HTML, each page in a module of its own, over the read models of `orca.views`; `orca.web.routes` says which path is which.
modules.description:
Every path answers HTML, or JSON to `Accept: application/json` or
`?format=json`, built from the same rows, so a script and a person see the
same thing (`orca.web.page.respond`). A page of something still going on
(a queued or running run, a running attempt) refreshes its live part from
a fragment path every few seconds (`_POLL` in `orca.ui.layout`), which
answers 286 once there's nothing more to show, and the page stops asking.
Beyond that, a few scripts are conveniences only: `/runs` filters as a
choice changes, Start runs updates its preview and command lines as you
type, and Cancel, rerun and rebuild ask before posting. Every form works
without them.

The run page and the pipeline page are a view (`orca.views.runs.RunView`,
`orca.views.pipelines.PipelineView`) drawn twice, as HTML here and as
JSON in `orca.api`, which `orca.web.routes` puts together. The other
pages still build their HTML and their JSON in one function, over the
rows of `orca.views`; they can be split the same way as they change.

| Module | |
|---|---|
| `orca.ui.home` | `/`: pipelines, recent runs, the timeline |
| `orca.ui.pipeline` | `/pipelines/<name>`: Overview, Runs and Operate, a key's page |
| `orca.ui.start` | Start runs, on the Operate tab |
| `orca.ui.coverage` | a pipeline's days or months and their state |
| `orca.ui.runs` | `/runs`: the runs list, a page at a time |
| `orca.ui.run` | `/runs/<id>`: a run's cards, steps, machines and files |
| `orca.ui.attempt` | an attempt's log and facts |
| `orca.ui.machines` | a run's machines and their metrics |
| `orca.ui.datasets` | datasets, a dataset, a snapshot's lineage, a rebuild |
| `orca.ui.ops` | Control, the watchdog, `/metrics`, and Fleet and Workers' redirects |
| `orca.ui.pools` | Ops' Pools: every pool's machines, a machine's page |
| `orca.ui.code` | `/code`: a file at a commit, coloured, for code on hover |
| `orca.ui.login` | the login page |
| `orca.ui.layout` | every page's frame and what pages draw with |
| `orca.ui.parts` | pieces several pages draw: cells, a runs table, facts |
| `orca.ui.step_cards` | a card per step, on hover |

modules.description:
A daily pipeline's card has two tabs, **Month** (a month of days) and
**Year** (twelve small months, each with how many of its days are done, and
a strip of every month of its range linking to their years). Both are in
the page; the links work without scripts (`?cov=month|year`, with `?cal=`
the month or year), and with them the tabs switch in place and the choice
is kept in `localStorage`, as the Steps tabs are. Year is the default. A
monthly pipeline's card is its year of months, as before, and an hourly
one's a day of hours (`?cal=YYYY-MM-DD`). For a sensor,
the days what it follows has but it hasn't done, failed or started are
`behind` (`orca.follow`), and `follow_html` is its Progress card's
Following line.

One calendar is read for both tabs (`year_calendar`): the month is cut out
of the year, so the card costs the same three queries as a month did.

What a card shows is in the page, so a hover asks nothing of the server: a
`<script type="application/json" class="step-cards">` in the Steps card
holds each step's `StepCard` (its kind, `after=`, function signature,
types, the datasets it reads and writes, where its code is, and on a
pipeline's page what its latest runs took and used) and, on a run's page,
each attempt's `AttemptCard`. An element with `data-step` (and on a run's
page `data-attempt`) shows the card of that step (and attempt), drawn by
`STEP_CARDS_JS`. The one thing fetched is the function's own signature and
docstring, from the source at the commit (`/code?u=&at=`, `def_summary`),
once per step per page; until it comes, or where the code can't be had, the
signature is the one `describe` records, its argument names orca's.

modules.summary: Two views `orca ui` draws in the browser: a run's Dista timeline, and the pipelines over time on the home page. Both are plain scripts in the page (nothing is fetched from elsewhere) over JSON the UI serves, and both load that JSON only when they're looked at, so the pages stay as fast as they were.
modules.description:
**A run's timeline** (`timeline_section`): the run's `timeline.json`
(Chrome's trace format, as dista writes it) drawn on a canvas, a track per
process (the driver or head first, then each worker) and a lane per slot
its spans overlap on, `X` and `B`/`E` events alike. Spans are coloured by
their function's name; "inputs" (a task waiting for what it reads) are thin
bars under them. A wheel zooms around the pointer, a drag zooms to what it
covers, and Reset zoom goes back; spans narrower than a pixel are drawn as
one pixel per lane, so a few hundred thousand events stay quick. Hovering
says the span's name, process and slot, start, duration and arguments. The
file is fetched when the section scrolls into view; Perfetto and the raw
file are linked beside it.

**The pipelines over time** (`gantt_tabs`, `gantt_panel`, `gantt_json`):
"List" and "Timeline" tabs over the home page's table, the choice kept in
`localStorage`; the list is the default and is all there is without
scripts. The timeline is a row per pipeline in the order of their datasets
(a pipeline that reads what another writes comes after it, indented by its
depth), its runs over the last hour, 6 hours, day or week as bars coloured
by status, fill runs thinner, a line at now, and a thin connector from a
run to each run its commits started (`orca.sensed` joined to
`orca.commits`). Datasets between pipelines are drawn at the left. Bars
narrower than two pixels are merged, and the JSON holds the newest
`MAX_RUNS` runs of the window.

```
GET /api/gantt?window=24h      # 1h, 6h, 24h or 7d
```

modules.summary: Ops' Pools (`/ops/pools`): every machine runs are placed on, one row each, by the pool a placement names.
modules.description:
| Pool | Kind | A machine is |
|---|---|---|
| `ec2` | EC2 | an instance orca launched for a run (`orca.instances`), live or ended in the last hour |
| `kubernetes` | k8s | a live run's pods (`orca-<run>-<start>`), on the Kubernetes runner: the runner records no pods or nodes, so the run is what there is |
| `worker:<pool>` | self-hosted | the machine a worker token's `orca worker` runs on (`orca.workers`), with the worker as columns of its row |

The scheduler's own machine (the local runner, and control-placed runs)
isn't a pool: it is Control (`/ops/control`).

A machine's state is `live`, `draining` (an EC2 worker the scheduler
drained) or `gone` (an instance that ended; a worker whose token was
revoked or expired, or that hasn't been seen for `ORCA_STALE_SECONDS`),
with what it's doing in `detail`. Like Fleet, a page view reads
`orca.instances`, `orca.fleet_samples`, `orca.workers` and `orca.runs`,
never a sampler's file.

modules.summary: Who a request is from, and whether it may act: the session cookie of a browser, the API token of a script (`orca --remote`), and the checks that keep another site's page from posting to the UI. Also the endpoints that log in and out. The users, sessions and audit rows themselves are `orca.auth`; API tokens are `orca.tokens`; a worker's token is checked by `orca.api.worker` instead, and gets nothing here.
modules.description:
| Path | |
|---|---|
| `/login` | `GET`: the form; `POST` `name`, `password`, `next`: a session, as the cookie `orca_session` |
| `/logout` | ends the session and clears the cookie |
| `/api/login` | JSON `name`, `password`, `label`, `days`: an API token for `orca login` |
| `/api/logout` | revokes the API token it's sent with |

A script's request is one with an `Authorization` header (or a JSON login
for a token). A browser sends neither to another site without a CORS
preflight, which the UI never answers, so a script's `POST` with no
`Origin` needn't be the UI's own; the token, not a cookie, is what it acts
with. A request with an `Authorization` header is answered 401 unless it's
a live token, whatever cookie it has.

modules.summary: Stopping `orca ui` without dropping a request. `docker stop` sends SIGTERM and waits 10 s before it kills; Ctrl-C sends SIGINT. Either one starts a drain:
modules.description:
1. `/healthz` answers 503 `draining` (the flag `Drain.draining` returns),
   so a health checker or proxy that asks over a kept-alive connection
   stops routing here; and the listening socket closes, so a new
   connection is refused at once (one waiting in its backlog is reset).
2. The requests already in the handler finish and their answers go out;
   so does one a kept-alive connection sends meanwhile.
3. Once no request has been in the handler for 200 ms, or after
   `ORCA_UI_DRAIN_SECONDS` (default 8, under `docker stop`'s 10), the
   server's loop stops, which closes the kept-alive connections, and
   `orca ui` exits 0. A request still running half a second after that
   can't be cut short (the handler runs on the loop's thread), so the
   process then exits 1 without it.

A second signal during the drain stops the loop at once.

A signal handler can't reach a Mojo variable, so it writes a byte to a pipe
whose write end is duplicated onto a fixed descriptor, `WAKE_FD`, and a
thread of its own waits on the read end (as `dista.signals` does for a
worker). The handler runs on whichever thread the kernel picks, and `write`
is async-signal-safe; `signal` installs it with `SA_RESTART`, so a query
it interrupts goes on.

Flare's `HttpServer.drain(timeout_ms)` always waits out its whole window,
since its loop publishes no count of what's in flight, so the drain counts
the requests in the handler itself (`Counting`) and stops the loop with
`HttpServer.close()` once there are none.

aliases.name: WAKE_FD
aliases.summary: The descriptor the handler writes to: below macOS's default limit of 256 open files, above what a process has open when it starts, and one below `dista.signals.WAKE_FD`.

structs.summary: `H`, counting the requests in it in `busy`.

overloads.signature: def __init__(out self, var inner: H, busy: AtomicCounter)

structs.name: Drain
structs.summary: A thread that drains the `HttpServer` it's given on SIGTERM or SIGINT, until this is dropped, which joins it. Serve the handler `counting` returns, so it knows what's in flight.

overloads.signature: def counting[H: Handler & Copyable](self, var handler: H) -> Counting[H]
overloads.summary: `handler`, counting its requests for the drain.
Set from the moment a drain starts; valid while this lives.
`ORCA_UI_DRAIN_SECONDS`, or 8 if it's unset or not a number; 0 stops without waiting for anything.

modules.summary: The router: a table of routes, each a method, a path pattern, what kind of request it is and the handler that answers it. `orca.web.routes` is the table; `orca.web.server` looks a request up here and wraps the handler in what its kind needs.
modules.description:
A pattern is the path's segments: a literal (`runs`), a parameter
(`{name}`: any segment but an empty one, URL-decoded) or a number
(`{id:int}`). A path matches a route of its length whose literals are its
segments and whose numbers parse. A path that would match but for a number
that isn't one (`/runs/x`, `/runs/1/attempts/x/log`) is answered 404,
"no run x", from the route's `noun`.

A `GET` route answers `HEAD` too. A read (`GET`) that matches nothing is
404, "nothing at <path>"; a `POST` that matches nothing is 405, since only
the actions take one, unless it's an action's but for its number, which
is 404.

modules.summary: Every path `orca ui` answers, and what answers it: the route table `orca.web.server` serves (`orca.web.router` for how a path matches).
modules.description:
Each handler here only takes the request's parameters out of the `Call`
and hands them to the page (`orca.ui`) or the action (`orca.api.actions`)
that does the work. A page answers HTML, or its JSON to `Accept:
application/json` or `?format=json` (`/api/...` always JSON). The worker
API (`/api/worker/...`) has a table of its own, `orca.api.worker`, and the
stylesheet is served before any route is looked up.

| Path | |
|---|---|
| `/` | pipelines, with their coverage (`orca.coverage`: partitions or keys done of those it has, `coverage` in the JSON), schedules, next runs and last runs |
| `/pipelines/<name>` | `?tab=overview` (default), `runs` or `operate`, each its own page; a pipeline's steps, partitions, schedule, next runs and runs; a keyed one's keys, done, live and failed; its fill (`orca.fill`): done of total, rate, ETA, today's estimated spend against its budget and why it's idle; its registration as `orca config show` prints it (`#config`, Overview); `?preview=1&partitions=` (`&rerun=1`): what Start runs would queue, queueing nothing; `?steps=graph` or `table`: the Steps tab shown without scripts |
| `/pipelines/<name>/progress` | the page's Progress card (runs going, fill, how far a sensor is behind what it follows (`orca.follow`), next run, coverage), as an HTML fragment the page refreshes every 5 s; `?tab=` is the tab polling it, which its "Log in to ..." links come back to |
| `/api/pipelines/<name>` | the same as JSON, whatever is asked for |
| `/pipelines/<name>/calendar` | a daily or monthly pipeline's days (months) of `?month=2023-01` (`2023`) with their state, as JSON: done, failed, live, open, outside; the page shows it as coverage (`?cal=` a month or year, `?cov=month` or `year`: a daily one's tab, year by default, both from one read of the year in `orca.ui.coverage`) and as the Start runs form's date picker |
| `/pipelines/<name>/keys/<key>` | one key of a keyed pipeline: its steps in every run it was in |
| `/runs` | runs, newest first, `?limit=` (or `?n=`; 50, at most 500) to a page; `?pipeline=`, `?status=` (one or more), `?trigger=`, `?from=`, `?to=`, `?since=`, `?key=` (a partition: a glob or a part), `?run=` (goes to that run); `?before=<id>`: the page older than that run, `?after=<id>`: the page newer than it (keyset, so pages stay put as runs arrive); the JSON's `next`, `prev` (and `next_url`, `prev_url`) are the cursors either side. A pipeline's Runs tab pages and filters the same, 20 to a page (`runs_page` in its JSON). Each status's count under the other filters is the JSON's `counts` |
| `/runs/table` | a runs list's page as the fragment it refreshes from: `?view=list` (`/runs`), `pipeline` (a pipeline's Runs tab) or `home` (recent runs), with the list's filters, `limit` and cursor; `X-Poll-Every` says when to ask again (5 s while a run on it is queued or running, 30 s on the newest page otherwise), and an older page with nothing going on answers 286 |
| `/home/pipelines` | the home page's table of pipelines, as the fragment it refreshes from (5 s while a run is queued or running, else 30 s) |
| `/runs/<id>` | a run's cards (Status, Partitions & trigger, Code, Resources, Settings), its steps (`?steps=table` (default), `timeline` or `graph`: the Steps tab shown without scripts), its machines, and the snapshots each step read and wrote |
| `/runs/<id>/attempts/<attempt>` | an attempt's log, with its error; its facts refresh from `/runs/<id>/attempts/<attempt>/facts` while it runs |
| `/code` | `?u=` a link to a file at a commit on GitHub: its lines and each coloured as HTML (`orca.highlight`), as JSON, for the code shown on hover; the UI fetches the file, so a browser needn't reach GitHub. With `&at=` a line, only that `def`'s signature, coloured, and its docstring's first paragraph, for a step's card (`orca.ui.step_cards`) |
| `/runs/<id>/timeline.json` | the run's Dista timeline, which its page draws (`orca.ui.viz`) and Perfetto opens |
| `/api/gantt` | the pipelines in dataset order with their runs over `?window=1h`, `6h`, `24h` (default) or `7d`, and the runs each started: the home page's Timeline tab (`orca.ui.viz`) |
| `/runs/<id>/driver.log` | the run's driver output, as the scheduler kept it |
| `/runs/<id>/metrics` | the run's machines: charts and peaks from its samples (`orca.metrics`) |
| `/ops` | redirects to `/ops/alerts`; "Ops" in the nav has Alerts, Control, Pools and Watchdog under it |
| `/ops/alerts` | Alerts (`orca.ui.alerts`): every alert sent (`orca.alerts`), newest first, 50 to a page (`?limit=`, at most 500; `?before=<id>`, `?after=<id>`), `?kind=` and `?state=open` or `resolved`; its kind, title and message, links, whether ntfy took it and whether it is still open; the newest page refreshes every 30 s from `/ops/alerts/live`; `/api/alerts` is the same as JSON |
| `/ops/control` | Control, the one machine running the scheduler, this UI, Postgres and local and control-placed runs (so not a pool on Pools): its own health: CPU, memory, the disk Postgres is on and network over `?range=24h`, `7d` or `14d`, and each container's memory (`orca.system`), and the watchdog's banner, refreshed every 30 s from `/ops/control/live`; `/api/system` is the same as JSON; `/system` redirects here (301) |
| `/metrics` | Prometheus gauges: the control instance's CPU, memory, disk, network and containers' memory, runs running and queued, hosts, and errors in the last hour; open like the other pages (reads need no login) |
| `/ops/pools` | Pools, every machine runs are placed on (`orca.ui.pools`, `orca.views.pools`): a row per EC2 instance orca launched (live, and gone for an hour after it ended), per live Kubernetes run's pods (on the Kubernetes runner) and per worker token's machine (`orca.workers`), with its pool, kind, state, image, CPUs, memory, runs, last heartbeat, CPU and worker; `?pool=` (`ec2`, `kubernetes`, `worker:<pool>`) and `?kind=` (`ec2`, `k8s`, `self-hosted`) filter it; with EC2 in view, Fleet's cards (`orca.fleet`) and its charts over `?range=24h` or `7d`; refreshed every 10 s from `/ops/pools/live`; `/api/pools` the same as JSON |
| `/ops/pools/<kind>/<id>` | a machine: its facts, and an EC2 instance's samples over its run (the run page's Machines charts) or the runs a worker claimed |
| `/ops/fleet`, `/ops/workers` | moved to `/ops/pools?kind=ec2` (Fleet's `?range=` kept) and `?kind=self-hosted` (301), as are `/ops/fleet/hosts`, `/ops/workers/live`, `/fleet` and `/fleet/hosts` (to `/ops/pools/live` for the fragments); asked for JSON, they answer Fleet's and Workers' JSON as before, as `/api/fleet` (the summary, hosts and charts of `orca.fleet`) and `/api/workers` (each worker token's pool, label, worker, image, last heartbeat, runs, CPUs and memory) do. A worker's own requests go to `/api/worker/...` with its token |
| `/watchdog`, `/api/watchdog` | the watchdog's rules with their last values, limits and snoozes, and the trips with a pipeline still paused (`orca.watchdog`); also the red banner on `/`, `/ops/pools` and `/ops/control`; the page refreshes every 30 s from `/watchdog/live` |
| `/datasets` | datasets, with their writers, readers and latest snapshots, and the graph of pipelines and datasets |
| `/datasets/<name>` | a dataset's place in that graph, the steps that write and read it (linked to their code), what a rebuild of it runs, and its snapshots; `?preview=1&partitions=`: a rebuild's runs by level, queueing nothing |
| `/datasets/<name>?before=<cursor>` | its snapshots 50 to a page, newest first; `?after=` for the newer page, the cursor `<attempt>.<snapshot>` (`snapshots_page` in the JSON) |
| `/datasets/<name>/snapshots/<id>` | a snapshot's lineage (`orca.lineage`): its diagram, Upstream (`back` in the JSON: the snapshot, if a run wrote it, and the snapshots it was written from, with the run and step that wrote each and what that step read) and Downstream (`forward`: the snapshots written from it) |
| `/rebuilds/<id>` | a rebuild's pipelines by level, with their runs (`orca.sensors`) |

The actions, each a `POST`, are `orca.api.actions`'; `/login`, `/logout`,
`/api/login` and `/api/logout` are `orca.web.auth`'s.

overloads.summary: The table, first match first.

modules.summary: `orca ui`'s server: one handler that looks each request up in the route table (`orca.web.routes`), checks who it's from (`orca.web.auth`) and answers it as its route's kind says.
modules.description:
```
ORCA_DATABASE_URL=postgresql:///orca ./build/orca ui     # 127.0.0.1:8270
```

A request goes through, in order:

1. The stylesheet, `/healthz` (200 once the database answers, without a
   login: what a deploy waits for before it retires the old UI; 503
   `draining` once a drain has started), and the
   worker API (`POST /api/worker/...`, `orca.api.worker`, its own token),
   answered before anything else.
2. The route. A `POST` that's no action, or another method than `GET`,
   `HEAD` or `POST`, is 405.
3. A `POST` whose `Origin` (or `Referer`) isn't the UI's own is refused
   (403), unless it's a script's with no `Origin` (`orca.web.auth`).
4. The database, per request; `/api/login` is answered here, before any
   token is looked at.
5. Who it's from: an API token or a session. A token that's no use is 401.
6. By the route's kind (`orca.web.router`): logging in or out as the
   handler says; a page with who's logged in (or a way to log in) in its
   header; an action, once login is on only with a session, audited as its
   user's.

The UI holds no state: its actions are rows the scheduler acts on, and it
can run beside the scheduler or anywhere else that reaches the database.
`ORCA_UI_ADDR` (`host:port`) moves it; it binds to localhost unless told
otherwise. `ORCA_WORKER_ADDR` serves the worker API on a listener of its
own as well (`orca.api.worker`). SIGTERM or SIGINT drains it: no new
connections, `/healthz` 503, the requests in flight answered, then exit 0 within
`ORCA_UI_DRAIN_SECONDS` (8; `orca.web.drain`).
